items.body:
In June, we reported that ICE was partnering with Tesco on the launch of autonomous cleaning robots across 600 Express stores. In doing so, the pair laid claim to the first deployment of this scale in the UK convenience sector.
The robots are now rolling out to a further 1,300 Express stores. These are designed as "co-bots" to work alongside Tesco colleagues. By taking over routine floor cleaning, they free up time for the store teams to focus on serving customers. The technology promises a consistent, premium clean every single day, backed by data tracking and reporting.
"From 600 Tesco Express stores to 1,900, this is a huge milestone for 2026. It’s always been about more than technology. It’s about making everyday tasks simpler for our colleagues and giving them more time to focus on our customers. Proud of everyone who helped make this happen and our partners ICE and Gausium," says Tabitha Gafencu, Project Manager - UK Stores Transformation Large and Convenience Format at Tesco.
Mark Bresnihan, CEO at ICE, says: "As long standing pioneers in cleaning technologies, ICE is delighted to partner with Tesco on this project. We are providing not just our industry leading autonomous machines, but also the comprehensive training and service support required to make this a success. Together, we are showing how data driven automation can work hand-in-hand with retail teams to improve cleaning standards."

items.body:
Cheryl Lynch has joined Tesco Technology as Head of Technology Operating Model. She joins from Cisco where she spent six years, serving as Senior Director. Her CV also includes a stint at Emirates.
In a LinkedIn post, she said: "And so the new chapter has begun...I have joined Tesco to head up Technology Operating Model a new and exciting role, which feels like the perfect fit. The role means spending time in the office and some time working from home and even better in the UK time zone. I couldn't be happier"
She added: "It's been an amazing week so far. I was up and running in 90 mins from walking in the door to sitting at a desk with my new laptop, fully authenticated and coffee in hand. Right, back to work!"
InPost
InPost recently reported a milestone with Tesco, installing its 1,650th locker across the grocery giant's UK estate to become its largest network with any single retail partner in the UK.
According to InPost's customer research, 66% of its locker users combine their visit with a Tesco shop and 53% now visit the retailer more often because of the locker. Satisfaction is high too, with 75% of users saying their visit was more convenient because of the locker, with the majority rating the service ten out of ten and stating they would recommend it to a friend or colleague.
The milestone builds on a partnership with Tesco that began in 2021, with InPost lockers now installed across the retailer's different store formats, from Express to Extra and Superstores.
Paul Selvey, Network Director at InPost UK, said: “Reaching this locker milestone with Tesco shows just how much shoppers value having real choice over how they collect, send and return parcels. For years, delivery has been designed around cost and convenience at checkout, not around what actually works for the consumer receiving the parcel. Putting lockers across Tesco Express locations to its Extra stores, means that choice is built into the consumer’s shopping journey itself, rather than bolted on as an afterthought."
Nick Burrows, Head of Property Income at Tesco, said: “We’re always looking for ways to make the shopping trip more convenient for customers. With 1,650 InPost lockers now available across Tesco stores, more customers than ever can collect, return or send parcels at a time that suits them, all from their local store. It’s another way we’re helping customers save time and fit everyday tasks around their busy lives."

items.title: New HyperFinity research highlights loyalty red flags driving shoppers away this Christmas
items.summary: 55% of UK shoppers say loyalty offers that are not relevant to them are a major frustration, making them the biggest red flag for retail loyalty programmes. That’s according to new research from HyperFinity.With retailers competing for customer spending during the crucial Christmas trading period, t
items.body:
55% of UK shoppers say loyalty offers that are not relevant to them are a major frustration, making them the biggest red flag for retail loyalty programmes. That’s according to new research from HyperFinity.
With retailers competing for customer spending during the crucial Christmas trading period, the findings highlight how poorly designed loyalty schemes risk undermining the relationships they are intended to build. Limited savings (35%), rewards that expire too quickly (29%), and rewards that change or are taken away (25%) are among the other frustrations putting shoppers off.
HyperFinity's report, produced with Bloomreach and Eagle Eye, surveyed 2,000 UK consumers who belonged to at least one of the 51 loyalty programmes featured in the company's March 2026 Retail Loyalty Index.
Analysis of the findings has identified three key areas where loyalty programmes are falling short of shopper expectations:
- Irrelevant offers: Generic promotions that fail to reflect individual shopping habits give customers little reason to engage with a loyalty programme or return to a retailer. Businesses need to understand what different customers value and make sure the offers they receive are relevant.
- Rewards that fail to deliver value: Loyalty benefits need to offer a clear and worthwhile return. If customers feel the savings are too small, or that spending more does not bring greater rewards, they have little incentive to engage with a scheme.
- Rewards that come with catches: Complicated conditions, short redemption windows and benefits that change or disappear can make schemes feel more difficult to use than rewarding. Retailers should make sure customers can understand, access and redeem the benefits they have been promised.
Thomas Hill, Co-founder and CCO at HyperFinity, says: “Christmas is a critical time for retailers, but it is also when customers have more reasons than ever to compare offers and decide where to spend. A loyalty programme should give people a genuine reason to come back, not just another card in their wallet or app on their phone."
"That means understanding what different customers value, making rewards relevant and ensuring the benefits on offer are actually worth having. Retailers that get this right have an opportunity to build stronger relationships beyond the festive period, while those that rely on generic offers risk giving customers very little reason to stay.”

items.title: E-commerce outsourcing Philippines: how agentic AI changes staffing, pricing, and operations in 2027
items.summary: For more than a decade, ecommerce brands relied on the Philippines for a simple operational formula: fluent English support, 24/7 holiday coverage, and a lower cost per contact than any domestic team could match. In 2027, agentic AI breaks that formula.Autonomous workflows now absorb routine WISMO (
items.body:
For more than a decade, ecommerce brands relied on the Philippines for a simple operational formula: fluent English support, 24/7 holiday coverage, and a lower cost per contact than any domestic team could match. In 2027, agentic AI breaks that formula.
Autonomous workflows now absorb routine WISMO (''where is my order?'') checks, standard return initiations, and basic catalogue lookups, and leave human specialists the exceptions that decide whether a customer comes back: fraud disputes, damaged freight claims, chargeback threats, and VIP retention. Gartner expects agents to resolve 80% of common service issues without a person by 2029; the e-commerce operators I work with are already halfway there.
I have watched this from both sides of the table. Over 40 years in outsourcing, including more than two decades as CX Strategist and EVP leading global business development at the world's largest contact center provider, I built and ran programs for eBay, Sears, T-Mobile, and Home Depot.
Then I co-founded Plant Addicts, a direct-to-consumer online retailer, and ran it as CEO, living the merchant's P&L, until it was acquired in 2025. At PITON-Global we now advise online retailers and marketplace brands on vetting, benchmarking, and contracting Philippine BPO partners under a vendor neutral model with zero markup on supplier rates. This is what we tell them about agentic era ecommerce outsourcing to the Philippines in 2027.
Why Does Agentic AI Change E-commerce BPO Staffing in the Philippines in 2027?
Agentic AI changes Philippine ecommerce staffing in 2027 by moving contact centers from high volume, single-skill Tier 1 queues to smaller, cross-trained exception pods that supervise AI actions and resolve high friction problems. With 60 to 75% of routine volume resolved autonomously, the human queue is harder, longer, and more consequential for customer lifetime value.
The arithmetic is simple and most RFPs still get it wrong. When the agent closes every delivery-window check and standard return before a person sees the ticket, what reaches the floor is the damaged pallet, the chargeback threat, and the customer who has already been through two bot loops (Figure 1).
In the legacy model, vendors staffed seasonal peaks with large cohorts trained on narrow scripts and measured on average handle time. In 2027, evaluating a partner on low AHT or cheap Tier 1 seats backfires: the easy calls have left the human queue, so average complexity and emotional temperature rise on every remaining interaction, and a specialist who is pushed to close in six minutes closes badly.
Figure 1. The taxonomy that should precede every 2027 RFP. The human lanes are small by volume and large by consequence.
This is also why e-commerce outsourcing to the Philippines looks different in 2027 from the voice heavy programmes I ran for eBay and Sears. The specialist we now staff is cross-trained across chat, email, SMS, voice, and marketplace messaging, carries six months or more on the brand's policies, holds the authority to approve a replacement or a goodwill credit inside a defined band, and is measured on whether the customer orders again. The country's advantage has moved up the queue with the work: fluent written English and a decade of marketplace experience matter more when every remaining ticket is an argument rather than a lookup. Table 1 sets the two models side by side.
Table 1. Four metrics that flip when the agent takes the routine volume. The buyer's job is to contract for the right-hand column.
How Are E-commerce BPO Pricing Models Shifting From Per-Hour Seats to Hybrid Outcomes?
E-commerce BPO pricing in 2027 is moving from pure hourly seat rates to hybrid structures that combine a transparent base staffing fee with resolution, CSAT, and retention-linked performance tiers. Per-hour pricing creates a built-in conflict once agentic AI shrinks total volume while making every human-handled ticket harder, and pure per-outcome pricing invites cherry-picking.
I learned the limits of outcome only pricing the hard way at Plant Addicts, where a per-resolution deal quietly turned every ambiguous shipping claim into a fast refund because a refund is a resolution. The model that works for a scaling 2027 program is the hybrid: a base rate that pays for a dedicated specialist pod, plus a bonus-malus band tied to first-contact resolution, CSAT, and the one number most contracts forget, refund leakage (Table 2). Attribution is the clause to fight over: a ticket the agent opened and a specialist closed counts for the specialist, and a ticket the specialist reopened after the agent "resolved" it counts against the agent's deflection rate, not the pod's FCR.
Table 2. The commercial models. The hybrid earns its complexity only if the contract says who gets credit for a ticket the agent started and a person finished.
Defeating the BPO "AI wrapper" markup
The trap in 2027 RFPs is the AI wrapper: a generalist BPO bundles an off-the-shelf third-party chatbot into its hourly rate and charges a 20 to 35 percent software premium without guaranteeing deflection or taking liability for a hallucinated policy promise. The answer is a Zero-Markup AI Transparency and IP Clause: technology licensing separated from human labour rates, pass-through pricing on third-party AI tools, and brand ownership of every custom prompt, disposition tree, and QA calibration rule built on your order data. When McKinsey maps the automation curve in agentic commerce , the merchants it expects to win are the ones whose returns logic and service rules are machine readable; you cannot make them machine-readable if your vendor owns them.
What Operational Controls, SLAs, and Guardrails Protect Margin and Brand Trust?
Protecting margin and customer trust in an agentic e-commerce operation takes strict limits on what the AI may approve alone, fast human escalation triggers, marketplace response-clock protection, and a contractual lock against post-pilot staffing dilution. An unguarded bot that issues refunds or misses platform windows during peak can erase a month of contribution margin in a weekend.
The stakes are not theoretical. Returns ran to an estimated $849.9 billion in 2025, with 19.3% of online sales coming back and roughly 9% of all returns fraudulent, by the National Retail Federation's count. Hand an agent authority over that flow without a cap and a human check, and the people gaming your return policy will find the cap for you. The six controls in Table 3 are the ones we write into every 2027 statement of work; the refund cap is first because it is the one that pays for the rest.
Table 3. The control set. Each benchmark is a starting point to tune against your own ticket history, not a universal constant.
Two of these deserve a word from the merchant's side of the desk. Marketplace response clocks are account health metrics on Amazon, Walmart, eBay, and TikTok Shop, not service metrics; one late or non-compliant bot reply can cost a seller its buy box in the week it can least afford. Refund leakage is where agentic programs quietly fail: the agent is calibrated to resolve, a credit resolves, and nobody audits the credits until the quarter closes.
Operations change shape with the controls. A Philippine supervisor's day in 2027 starts with the agent's overnight action log rather than a queue report, QA calibrates AI transcripts and human escalations in the same weekly session, and workforce planning forecasts exceptions per thousand orders instead of contacts per hour. A provider that cannot show you those three artifacts is running a 2019 floor with a chatbot bolted on.
How Should an Online Retailer Sequence a 2027 Roll-out Ahead of Peak?
Sequence a 2027 e-commerce outsourcing program backward from Cyber Five: audit 90 days of tickets into AI deflectable, AI assisted, and human only lanes before writing the RFP, run a 30-to-45-day controlled pilot with 10 to 20 specialists, stress-test escalation thresholds and marketplace clocks 60 days out, and freeze changes two weeks before go-live.
Peak is the test every 2027 programme is really built for. Adobe counted $257.8 billion of US online holiday spending in 2025, $44.2 billion of it in the five days from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday, with traffic from generative AI sources to retail sites up 693 percent year over year. The shoppers arriving through an AI assistant expect the merchant's support to be as fluent as the assistant that sent them, and the returns wave that follows lands on the same team. Figure 2 is the sequence we use with clients; the dates are counted back from Cyber Five because that is the deadline nobody can move.
Figure 2. The roll-out, to scale. The pilot ends before the freeze on purpose: a program still calibrating refund thresholds in November is a programme calibrating them on live margin.
Three choices carry most of the risk. First, the taxonomy audit comes before the RFP, not after, because a vendor cannot price a human queue it has never seen. Second, the pilot pod sits in Metro Manila or Cebu with a named lead, and the cohort lock in Table 3 is signed before a single seat is added. Third, multi-site continuity is not optional: a primary Manila hub paired with Cebu or Iloilo delivery and a tested remote failover means a typhoon or a grid outage never interrupts live checkout or post-purchase support.
At PITON-Global we run the taxonomy audit and the pilot benchmark with the client, then shortlist providers that have already passed both; the provider that wins pays our fee, and nothing is added to the rate card.
Frequently Asked Questions
Will agentic AI eliminate e-commerce BPO jobs in the Philippines in 2027?
No. It eliminates repetitive Tier 1 ticket volume and shifts Philippine e-commerce teams toward higher skilled exception handling, marketplace dispute resolution, and proactive customer retention, with fewer seats per million orders and a higher value per seat.
What is the biggest hidden cost in AI enabled e-commerce outsourcing?
Two things that compound each other: uncontrolled refund leakage from poorly calibrated automation that issues unnecessary credits or creates repeat contacts, and vendor "AI wrapper" markups that charge inflated seat rates for a generic bot nobody is accountable for.
How should online retailers prepare for Q4 peak volume under an agentic AI model?
Lock in a core year round Philippine specialist pod, stress-test AI escalation thresholds and marketplace response clocks 60 days ahead of Cyber Five, freeze rubric and threshold changes two weeks out, and contract pre-certified reserve cohorts instead of relying on last minute seasonal hiring.
About the author
John Maczynski is CEO of PITON-Global, a vendor neutral BPO advisory firm that helps e-commerce and retail brands select, benchmark, and govern outsourcing partners in the Philippines.
A 40-year outsourcing veteran, he previously served as CX Strategist and Executive Vice President at the world's largest contact centre provider, where he led global business development for more than two decades and built programs for eBay, Sears, T-Mobile, and Home Depot. He also co-founded and ran Plant Addicts as CEO, a direct-to-consumer online retailer acquired in 2025, which gave him a merchant's view of fulfilment exceptions, refund economics, and what a peak season does to a support queue.

items.title: Next data accessed in cyber breach
items.summary: The fashion retailer says there is no evidence customers' personal data was compromised.
items.body:
Next data accessed in cyber breach
- Published
Next has said that some of its data has been accessed in a cyber breach affecting a third-party online supplier.
The high street retailer said there was no evidence that customers' personal data had been compromised.
The firm - which has its headquarters in Enderby, Leicestershire - said it had been informed by one of its suppliers about the incident, which led to "unauthorised access to certain benign data relating to Next".
"We took immediate steps to investigate the nature and scope of the incident with the supplier," the company told investors.
"Our investigations are ongoing. However, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised.
"The information affected is limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or Next."
The company added it was treating the situation "with the utmost seriousness", and working with the supplier as well as the police and regulators.
Next is the latest retailer to be caught up in a cyber breach.
In October, Asos said an "unauthorised party" had gained access to an employee's account, leading customers to receive a phone alert saying that the retailer had been hacked.
The firm said the attacker gained access to some personal data, including names and contact details belonging to customers.
In 2025 Marks & Spencer suffered from a major cyber-attack, which forced it to stop all online sales for about six weeks and led to some empty shelves in shops.

items.title: Lidl: Britain can't afford to throw away 'generation of talent' and Labour must get on with a youth jobs shake-up
items.summary: As the Treasury puts up resistance to employer tax cuts designed to get young people back to work, the discount supermarket has said Milburn reforms must not be stalled.
items.body:
Lidl: Britain can’t afford to throw away ‘generation of talent’ and Labour must get on with a youth jobs shake-up
A top Lidl executive has said Britain can’t afford to throw away a ‘generation of talent’ as she urged Labour to get on and implement a youth jobs shake-up.
As the Treasury puts up resistance to tax cuts for employers designed to get young people back to work, the discount supermarket has said Milburn reforms must not be stalled.
Retailers have called on the Government to reverse hefty tax increases so they can employ more young people at a time when 13.5 per cent of people aged 16-24 in the UK are classed as ‘Neets’ – not in employment, education or training.
Published last week, Alan Milburn’s review told ministers to take a ‘full throttle’ response to the crisis and roll back changes to National Insurance contributions (NICs).
Milburn urged Labour to double the salary threshold for employer National Insurance for entry-level jobs for young people in retail and hospitality, from £5,000 to £10,000.
This would represent a major U-turn after Rachel Reeves lowered the threshold at which employers start paying the levy from £9,100 to £5,000.
Lidl is among retailers to back calls for the Government to roll back changes to employer National Insurance contributions
Writing in the Daily Mail, Stephanie Rogers, chief people officer at Lidl GB, said that ‘too many young people are still locked out of the job market’.
She said: ‘Taking that first step into work is daunting without prior experience, and we cannot afford to let a generation of talent stall before it has begun.’
Urging ministers to act on the proposals ‘as soon as possible’, Rogers said that ‘young people out of work today cannot afford a slow rollout’ of changes to help retailers hire.
Milburn’s ‘call for a complete system reset’ was ‘critical’, she said.
She said that NICs changes plus other recommendations, such as £3,000 hiring incentives for young people who have been out of work or training for six months, were the ‘right practical levers to turn the tide’.
Retailers must help the Government ‘by backing potential over a polished CV’, she added. Lidl has started to recruit some 18-21-year-olds out of education or work, giving them funded placements, as part of the Government’s Youth Guarantee Scheme.
She added: ‘Getting young people through the door is only the start. To make the review’s ambition a reality, we urge the Government to bring forward the required reforms without delay.
‘By pairing swift policy action with sustained employer investment, we can ensure that young colleagues don’t just find a first job - they build a lasting career.’
Her remarks echo the urgency expressed by other retail chiefs, including the boss of Marks & Spencer, who has accused the Government of staging one of the ‘biggest tax grabs in history’.
Stuart Machin dismissed the Budget as ‘a whole lot of nothing’ after the Government ignored his calls to reverse rises to NICs, which he said had made it harder for firms to hire young people.
Before the Budget, Machin called on the Chancellor to reverse ‘the mistakes of the last two Budgets’.
Harvir Dhillon, lead economist at the British Retail Consortium, said that the Government must implement the NICs changes as soon as possible to ‘help ease employment costs just as inflationary pressures build.’
Stephanie Rogers, Chief People Officer at Lidl GB, says the retailer 'strongly urges' ministers to act to help unemployed young people.
Government must act 'without delay' to help young people into work
Stephanie Rogers, Chief People Officer at Lidl GB
At Lidl GB, a fifth of our workforce is under 25, and every day across our stores, warehouses and offices, I see the energy and fresh perspective these young people bring to our business.
Yet across Britain, too many young people are still locked out of the job market. Taking that first step into work is daunting without prior experience, and we cannot afford to let a generation of talent stall before it has begun.
That is why Alan Milburn’s call this week for a complete system reset to get more young people into sustained work is so critical. The review sets out the right practical levers to turn the tide – from £3,000 hiring incentives for young people who have been out of work or training for six months, to raising employer National Insurance thresholds for 21 to 24-year-olds in retail and hospitality. But young people out of work today cannot afford a slow rollout. We therefore strongly urge ministers to move on Milburn’s recommendations as soon as possible.
We recognise that the Government cannot achieve a system reset on its own. If we want a stronger economy, employers must also play their part by backing potential over a polished CV. At Lidl, we are already showing what works when you create multiple routes into employment.
Through the Government’s Youth Guarantee Scheme – which connects 18 to 21-year-olds out of education or work with funded placements – we have recruited our first colleagues into our stores, with plans underway to welcome many more. We are not just offering a placement, but industry-leading training and a supportive environment where young people develop transferable skills to secure their future.
This sits alongside our wider push to remove barriers to employment. Earlier this year, in partnership with the Department for Work and Pensions, we began ringfencing 10 per cent of interview slots for every new store – and at least 480 across our warehouses – for people out of work for six months or more. By fast-tracking candidates straight to interview without a CV, we give them the chance to show what they can bring, in person.
Meanwhile, our market-leading Degree Apprenticeships in Retail Leadership and IT offer an outstanding alternative to traditional university routes, allowing colleagues to earn while they learn and graduate with a BSc (Hons) degree, heaps of hands-on experience and zero tuition debt.
Getting young people through the door is only the start. To make the review’s ambition a reality, we urge the Government to bring forward the required reforms without delay. By pairing swift policy action with sustained employer investment, we can ensure that young colleagues don’t just find a first job – they build a lasting career.

items.body:
Debenhams Group, home to Debenhams, Karen Millen, boohoo, MAN and PrettyLittleThing, has announced an AI powered Gift Finder on WhatsApp.
Powered by Meta's AI technology, the experience is designed to make online shopping feel more personal, giving customers the kind of tailored assistance they might expect from speaking to a sales assistant in-store, but through WhatsApp.
A pilot launched ahead of Black Friday and the Christmas shopping period. Customers can access this through adverts on Facebook and Instagram or by scanning a QR code, which all direct them to a WhatsApp conversation with a business agent. From there, they can share who they're buying for, their budget and any preferences to receive tailored product recommendations from Debenhams' range.
The Gift Finder will show customers relevant products alongside their current sale prices, allowing them to explore different options and select their favourites. Once they've chosen their gifts, customers will receive a personalised link taking them directly to the Debenhams website, with their selected products already added to their basket.
Dan Finley, CEO at Debenhams Group, says: “AI is opening up new possibilities for making shopping more personal and intuitive, helping customers find the right products with less effort and greater confidence. With our WhatsApp Gift Finder, we’re working with Meta to put that into practice, giving shoppers tailored gifts for friends and family on a platform they already use."
“This latest collaboration reflects our drive to be at the forefront of retail innovation, putting emerging technology into customers’ hands and helping shape the next generation of shopping.”

items.title: Poundland is facing collapse - what's gone wrong?
items.summary: Poundland has a matter of days to find a buyer or face collapsing into administration. Why?
items.body:
Poundland is facing collapse - what's gone wrong?
- Published
The future of Poundland hangs in the balance as it faces a possible collapse into administration.
Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.
Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.
If it were to collapse, the jobs of its 11,000 employees would be at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.
How have we got here?
Have people stopped shopping at Poundland?
People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.
Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for Â£1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a Â£68m loss to an Â£18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.
Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of Â£1.9m were up Â£1.2m on last year.
Halloween sales were 11.4% higher than last year - this is usually a good indicator of how a retailer will do at Christmas, says retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth of Savvy Marketing.
According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor: "This isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland. The tills are busier than they were a year ago."
She adds: "On the face of it, a turnaround seems well under way."
However, Gordon Brothers has been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.
It had frozen about Â£50m in funds leading to concerns Poundland's shops would run out of stock.
Gordon Brothers released around Â£21m over two weeks recently, giving the chain a little more breathing space.
So why is it facing administration?
Poundland seems to be facing "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", Palmer says.
However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams says the business is making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".
It says it has provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.
It has also made about Â£18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.
As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a Â£22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for Â£1.
As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.
"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."
Irish firm Martin Property Group has offered to buy the business as a going concern, while London-based holding company Xyra Group has also made a rescue bid, although doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer.
A German investment firm, Zachert Private Equity, is also understood to have made a late offer.
Gordon Brothers has also been weighing options to break Poundland up.
The US company's view is that ultimately breaking the retailer up will provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate will also have to agree to keep the employees on.
Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale say it is driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.
But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim.
What future does Poundland have?
For now, Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended by 10 days to find a rescue deal.
Shuttleworth says the future of Poundland is "really unclear, with the owners and the management at loggerheads about its future".
Palmer says there are two ways forward for Poundland - either a solvent deal, where the company gets bought and carries on trading, or a collapse followed by a break-up.
"The immediate make-or-break issue is Christmas: a value retailer that can't get stock on its shelves in November and December is in serious trouble, whatever its full-year results say," says Palmer.
There has been political pressure on Gordon Brothers from both Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds. They have called for answers over why the Martin Property Group offer to buy the business, which would have protected jobs, was rejected.
A committee of MPs also questioned Gordon Brothers last week, adding to pressure.
But Shuttleworth says that as a US firm Gordon Brothers appears "unmoved" by the arguments that the UK government has put forward.

items.title: Here's why Walmart should pilot Ocado Group's game changing online grocery fulfilment technology
items.summary: Ocado Group just raised the bar for in-store online grocery fulfilment. So says Brittain Ladd, a supply chain consultant and former Amazon executive.Ladd made the claim in relation to Ocado Innovation, part of Ocado Group, recently being granted U.S. Patent 12,798,878 B2 for a storage and retrieval
items.body:
Ocado Group just raised the bar for in-store online grocery fulfilment. So says Brittain Ladd, a supply chain consultant and former Amazon executive.
Ladd made the claim in relation to Ocado Innovation, part of Ocado Group, recently being granted U.S. Patent 12,798,878 B2 for a storage and retrieval system that presents inventory totes at two heights within a single picking workstation. Each level has its own conveyor, drop-off column, and return column. The patent drawings show one associate reaching both totes from the same standing position.
In a LInkedIn post, Ladd commented: "The operating logic is simple. While an associate picks from one tote, the other conveyor can move a tote out and bring the next one into position. If waiting for inventory is what slows the picker down, a steadier flow of totes can help the same associate pick more items per hour."
"Ocado has described SBA as a compact automated fulfilment system that can sit inside or alongside a grocery store. The patented workstation fits that strategy. It could give a grocer more picking capacity in a space where every square foot competes with selling space, inventory, and order staging."
"Retailers are searching for in-store automation because they want to fulfill more pickup and delivery orders from the stores they already operate. That’s where I think Ocado has raised the bar."
Compared to SymMicro from Symbotic, and other in-store automation solutions, Ocado’s SBA appears to have the most capabilities, Ladd believes. When combined with their CFCs, Ocado offers a supremely capable automation solution for retailers, he argues.
He concluded: "Symbotic continues to “struggle” with their SymMicro test site inside a Walmart DC located in Raymond, NH. Symbotic’s RDC Gen 2 is also “behind schedule” according to sources I’ve spoken with. I strongly recommend that Walmart should pilot Ocado’s SBA solution. I also encourage Walmart to push Symbotic and SoftBank to assess an acquisition of Ocado. Walmart can’t keep waiting."

items.body:
Victoria Dunn is starting a new position as Loyalty Operations & Integration Lead at John Lewis Partnership.
She joins from Asda where she spent 11 and a half years, most recently serving as Head of Loyalty Propositions & Operations.
Asda
Asda has partnered with Rokt to deliver relevant offers to its customers at checkout across its online grocery business and George, its clothing and home brand. Using Rokt Pay+ on the payment page and Rokt Thanks on the order confirmation page, Asda says it has created a new retail media revenue stream at the point of purchase, while customer conversion remains unchanged.
Rokt uses AI to determine the most relevant next action for each customer in real-time on both the payments and confirmation pages.
“Checkout is a critical part of the customer journey, so we were deliberate about how we approached it,” says Chris Chalmers, Vice President Customer Data and Loyalty at Asda “The results show we can make that experience more relevant for customers while creating meaningful new value for the business.”
Asda first launched Rokt Thanks on George’s order confirmation page in January 2025. It added Rokt Pay+ to the payment page and then expanded both products across its online grocery business. The results include: Rokt revenue on George more than doubled after Rokt Pay+ was added. Pay+ now makes up 51% of Rokt revenue on George, and 36% across groceries and George. Rokt revenue on Asda's grocery business grew 54% year on year, based on a 30-day comparison. Customer conversion was unaffected across both businesses.
“The payment page is one of the highest intent moments in e-commerce, but historically it’s been largely untapped,” says Courtney Hopkins, SVP of Strategic Partnerships at Rokt
“Asda is showing that retailers can improve the experience for customers, thereby creating meaningful incremental value in that moment. We look forward to continuing to innovate and grow the partnership to unlock even greater relevance throughout the e-commerce journey and potentially even customer acquisition.”

items.title: Teens more likely to shop in person than their elders thanks to Instagram posts and matcha
items.summary: Youngsters are being drawn to malls, retail parks and high streets by online food and fashion posts, such as those by Marks & Spencer's unlikely viral sensation Kathryn Turner.
items.body:
Teens more likely to shop in person than their elders thanks to Instagram posts and matcha
Research shows teenagers are more likely to shop in-person than their elders.
They are being drawn to malls, retail parks and high streets by viral food and fashion posts, such as those for Marks & Spencer and beauty chain Sephora.
Two in five 12 to 20-year-olds say they shop mostly or entirely 'IRL' (or in real life), against a third of Gen Z and Millennials, according to shopping mall owner Hammerson and consultancy Retail Economics.
There have been many reports of Chinese online retailers Shein and Temu undercutting British retailers, who are made to pay high business rates on physical properties, while online sellers dodge customs duty on parcels under £135.
The Government has been slow to crack down on this loophole.
But, offsetting this, Rob Wilkinson, boss of Hammerson, which owns Birmingham's Bullring, Bristol's Cabot Circus and Manchester Arndale, said: 'Gen Alpha may be the most digitally native generation yet, but digital discovery is driving them into physical destinations, not away from them.
'They still want to shop, meet friends and spend time together in person.'
Matcha: The popular green drink which is sold at cafes such as Blank Street (pictured) is encouraging younger shoppers on to the high street
Some 76 per cent of Gen Alpha have hit the shops after being prompted by social media at least once in the past year, the study shows.
An example is M&S Food's director of product development Kathryn Turner, who has become a viral sensation on Tiktok and Instagram of late.
Her posts drive shoppers to seek out the foods she recommends in its stores.
And those who make regular shopping trips based on what they see online spend more than twice as much in-store as others, according to the Hammerson research.
Youngsters influenced online are estimated to spend over £1,600 a year in shops selling goods other than food.
Retailers are paying attention to this demand, as Gen Alpha could spend £5.3billion a year.
Sephora, owned by French giant LVMH, is planning to open ten more shops in the UK over the next year, bringing its total to 28.
Its arrival at the Bullring helped drive more than one million extra customer visits in its first year.
Another thing encouraging teens into shops is 'unusual' flavours of matcha.
Matcha is a popular caffeinated green drink, made popular by coffee chains such as Blank Street and Joe & the Juice.
Wilkinson said: 'People are looking for destinations that give them compelling reasons to visit, and we are evolving our destinations to reflect this: from the brands we bring into the mix of food, entertainment and experiences we offer.'
Scam fears give boost to real-world shopping
The fear of being scammed when shopping online is also driving shoppers to the high street, according to new research.
Nationwide predicts that people will redirect an average of £129 to spend on the high street rather than online in this year's Black Friday sales, while 14 per cent of have changed where they shop out of fear.
More than a quarter say they have become more cautious about clicking links in emails, texts or social media posts, in the wake of increasing cyber attacks in recent weeks.
Almost a quarter have spent more time researching a retailer or offer before buying, while 21 per cent have delayed making a purchase until they could check it was genuine.

items.title: Black Friday online scam fears will see worried shoppers spend £129 more on the high street instead
items.summary: Research by Nationwide shows people are delaying, avoiding or redirecting an average of £129, while 14 per cent of have changed where they shop out of fear.
items.body:
Black Friday online scam fears will see worried shoppers spend £129 more on the high street instead
Millions of shoppers will be looking to bag themselves a bargain this Black Friday as retailers slash product prices.
In the past decade, the event has cemented itself as the start of the Christmas shopping season and has become the busiest time for purchases in the entire year.
On Black Friday last year, which was November 28, Nationwide said it was the busiest day for card payments.
Britain's biggest building society predicts customers will make almost 44million transactions across Black Friday to Cyber Monday, up 9 per cent compared with 2025 – to reach a record high.
But while many will take the opportunity to try and bag a bargain, Nationwide said more people this year are staying vigilant of scammers when shopping online.
Its research predicts that people will redirect an average of £129 to spend on the high street instead, while 14 per cent of have changed where they shop out of fear.
Fresh fears: Black Friday shoppers to spend money in-store and avoid online scams
More than a quarter say they have become more cautious about clicking links in emails, texts or social media posts, in the wake of increasing cyber attacks in recent weeks.
And almost a quarter have spent more time researching a retailer or offer before buying, while 21 per cent have delayed making a purchase until they could check it was genuine.
A similar number have avoided making a purchase entirely.
Purchase scams are the most popular type of scam, transaction data spanning September to December 2025 shows.
This is when shoppers buy an item that's fake, doesn't really exist or through a social media ad, online marketplace or cloned website.
Purchase scams have increased by 19 per cent compared with the same period in 2024 and now make up 67 per cent of cases.
Customers aged 18 to 24 accounted for 15 per cent of all cases, the highest case volume by age and scam type.
Advance fee scams have also increased by 44 per cent. This is when fraudsters demand an upfront payment for something that never arrives.
Examples include fake jobs, loan-fee, prize, inheritance and customs scams.
While investment scams were less common, they had the highest average value over the same time period.
Investment scams involving 55 to 64-year-olds accounted for 10 per cent of total transaction value, the highest transaction value by age and scam type.
Gareth Pindred, fraud director at Nationwide, said: 'Purchase scams were by far the most common scam during the 2025 festive period, but a sharp rise in advance fee scams shows why we must stay alert to other types too.
'Our research shows scam concerns are prompting some people to avoid purchases or shop elsewhere.
'If you're unsure, pause, speak to a friend or check any suspicious payments with your bank.'

items.title: Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
items.summary: We put four AI models to the test to see if they could save us money on a new TV.
items.body:
Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
- Published
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.
Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.
It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.
But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.
Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.
A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.
Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.
But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.
Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.
In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.
But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.
We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.
While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.
ChatGPT - full price and not available to buy
OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.
Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for Â£499 down from Â£649.
The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from Â£379 to Â£814.
Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at Â£649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.
This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.
But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.
The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, Â£150 over our budget and not available online.
At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a Â£1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".
Claude - honest, but not too helpful
Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.
Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.
It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.
But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.
Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.
Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.
It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".
We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.
Gemini - a familiar pattern
Different AI model, same TV manufacturers - albeit different Hisense and TCL models to the previous chatbots' recommendations.
Gemini generated a table comparing four different models, but offered no links to the stores it named, so we searched for them ourselves.
The prices for one TCL TV were correct at Â£649, but it was sold out at one of the named retailers.
It said the other TCL model was available from Argos and Currys for Â£539 - correct for Argos, but when we checked Currys, it was Â£60 more expensive.
Again, it included two Samsung models to avoid due to lower screen specs.
Alexa - accurate but limited
Alexa came back with four TVs, from its own Amazon Ember at Â£532 to a Â£699 Samsung.
But its top recommendation was to go for another Samsung model at Â£616 (down from Â£749), based on its picture quality and Amazon customer rating.
Its fourth option was for a Sony TV, but it was only 50 inches, leaving us unsure why it had included it.
All the prices stated were correct, but Amazon only searches its own store. Alexa did acknowledge this, encouraging us to check its rivals for better deals, "as prices can vary" and we could get longer guarantees elsewhere.
Inconsistent pricing
There are methods that can boost the likelihood of getting a better response, from crafting more informative prompts to upping a chatbot's "thinking" level.
Tech journalist Alex Hughes had better luck than we did when he used ChatGPT's agentic AI mode to find a TV in last year's Black Friday sales.
Agentic AI is still in its early days, but it allows AI to act with more autonomy and carry out multi-step tasks.
The search took about 20 minutes "with very little work on my end needed," Hughes wrote for Tom's Guide, external in November 2025.
A year on, he told the BBC he didn't go through with buying a TV at that time.
He did later purchase one of the seven models ChatGPT had surfaced - but he had found it for a lower price in a bricks-and-mortar shop.
Will he be using AI to find Black Friday deals again this year? "Probably not," he said.
He reckoned it saved him time, but "when you're trying to deal with something like live price data... it will be inconsistent and quite often incorrect".
Slim pickings
While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.
Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.
If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".
"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.
Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.
Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".
But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work, external to Black Friday deal-hunting.
"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under Â£400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.
"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."

Further products in the range include Baileys Chocolate Caramel Whirls, launched last year, which come both singly (£1) and in three-packs (£2.75), and Original Irish Cream Truffles (£5.25). The Baileys Chocolate Collection… This story continues at Baileys chocolate includes advent calendar in 2026 Christmas line-up Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Further products in the range include Baileys Chocolate Caramel Whirls, launched last year, which come both singly (£1) and in three-packs (£2.75), and Original Irish Cream Truffles (£5.25).
The Baileys Chocolate Collection Box (175g) will also be back, an assortment of milk, white and dark chocolates tasting of Baileys Original Irish Cream with luxury fillings.
Completing the range are the Baileys Christmas Tree Truffle Tin (228g) and Baileys Christmas Truffle Box (100g), both filled with Baileys’ Original Irish cream truffles and new packaging for 2026 featuring a winter scene.
Ethan Duffey, brand manager at Lir Chocolates, said: “Christmas remains the biggest opportunity for premium chocolate and our 2026 Baileys Chocolate collection has been developed to help retailers maximise every gifting and self-treat occasion throughout the season.
“With the introduction of our first Baileys Chocolate Advent Calendar and the return of Baileys Whirls following a strong first year in 2025, the range combines exciting new formats with proven favourites.
“Supported by the strength of Baileys as a household brand, the collection brings together new launches and festive favourites to offer consumers even more ways to enjoy the iconic Baileys taste at Christmas.”
Baileys Chocolate is made in Ireland by Lir Chocolates, which specialises in developing hand-crafted chocolates.
Products are available to independent retailers via wholesalers including Hancocks.

items.title: EU wants ‘closest possible relationship’ with UK after agreeing Brexit reset deal – live
items.summary: President of European Council says EU ‘remains open to have the closest possible relationship’ with the UK Senior correspondent Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said. Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months , a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China. But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today. This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state. It was the same poi
items.body:
European council president says EU wants the 'closest possible relationship' with the UK
On the UK’s broader deliberations about its long-term relationship with the EU, Costa says diplomatically:
“We respected the sovereign decision taken by the British people in 2016, and I recall the words of the European Council after the referendum: we regret, but we respect. And we will equally respect whatever decision the United Kingdom takes about the future of its long term relationship with the European Union.”
He says the EU “remains open to have the closest possible relationship” with the UK.
But he also pointedly says, “you know our principles well,” including “the indivisibility of all of our four freedoms of the single markets.”
How to read EU-UK reset declaration on youth mobility, three sectoral deals and others - analysis
Jakub Krupa
The main document from today’s summit is this one: the joint declaration signed by the two sides.
Fancy reading it with me? Let’s go.
I won’t read it chronologically, but jump a bit, reflecting what I think you are looking for, and not how the document is written.
On “people to people” relations (pages 7-8), the document confirms the Youth Experience Scheme (YES) that will allow “100,000 people from the EU and the UK respectively to reside for up to three years to engage in activities such as work, studies, au-pairing, volunteering or simply travelling.”
On timing, it says the sides “aim to apply this agreement no later than 2028,” and want it to kick in “no later than January 2030.” It will apply to those up to the age of 31, so effectively will help those born in 1999 and later.
The document also confirms the UK’s return to the Erasmus+ programme in 2027, which we already knew about.
On the thorny issue of tuition fees, it says the parties will “work towards a supplementing agreement” to be agreed within six months. It’s very much unfinished business on that point.
In a win for artists and performers, the document also includes a somewhat vague, but promising, commitment to “explore further mutually beneficial solutions” to help touring artists with ridiculous red tape currently in place.
The statement also covers some of the key sectoral deals we mentioned earlier (pages 9-10),on emissions trading systems, sanitary and phytosanitary measures (SPS), and yes – of course – on fish (noting the decision on full reciprocal access to waters to fish until 30 June 2038).
In similarly practical decisions, there is also a note on “the significant progress achieved in discussions on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications for architects” which are set to continue.
The statement also covers important issues on judicial and security matters, noting plans to enhance cooperation between law enforcement agencies and, particularly, on the removal of foreign national offenders and migrant returns (pages 11-12).
The new language on economic resilience and cooperation is on pages 13-14, including commitment to “counter technology leakage in critical sectors, mitigate risks to critical infrastructure, and [to build] resilient supply chains” and so on.
The document, finally, also covers foreign and defence policy, in generally vague language, but across several pages (1-7).
It includes a long list of things the EU and the UK agree on, including on their support for Ukraine, foreign and defence policy priorities related to Africa, Arctic, Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Nato, Moldova, and the Western Balkans.
It also includes a line on commitment to “effective multilateralism” through the UN, the international criminal court, which continues to attract attacks from the US, and the global rules-based trade system.
And then we are back to questions on today’s deal and the tuition fees disagreement – and whether the two EU leaders agree with Burnham that today’s deal marks the high point of what can be done without a broader vision for the EU-UK relationship.
Costa smiles and says that the focus needs to be on building “the closest relationship possible” between the EU and the UK, but how close it can get needs to be defined by the British.
“In the meantime, we need to work very hard to try to solve problems to our companies, to our citizens, to improve the competitiveness of our economies,” he says.
But, somewhat echoing Burnham’s language earlier (14:37), he focuses on younger generations and says “these young people, a large part of them, was not here ten years ago, but they are here today.”
“And this is our duty to open to them new opportunities,” he says.
He says today’s deal on youth mobility for 100,000 people “is the best way to give future to our shared values, our mutual interest, our historic bond and cultural values that we share together.”
Von der Leyen says “we can always work on an incremental improvement to our relationship,” but she agrees that there is a much broader question on “the wider picture, the bigger picture” of how Europe should respond to “dramatic and big changes globally.”
Burnham, EU leaders condemn 'utterly unacceptable' Russian incursion into Polish airspace
The next question is on something very different – on continuing hybrid attacks about different European countries, asked in the context of airspace violations in Poland.
Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone are reported to have crashed in Poland during Russian air attacks on Ukraine that took place amid major western military exercises by allied countries.
All three speakers condemn the incident.
EU’s Costa says “it shows that, unfortunately, Russia instead of showing willingness to engage in peace talks continue to spread the threats.”
“This is very dangerous and shows Russia is going in the wrong direction,” he says.
Von der Leyen strikes a similar line.
Burnhamsays the incursion into Polish airspace is “utterly unacceptable,” as he says he wants to send “a strong message of solidarity to prime minister Tusk and the Polish people who we will support, always, in any way that we can.”
He makes a broader point on the back of that, saying “Europe is becoming more coordinated in terms of defence and security,” and today’s agreement helps with that.
He pivots to Ukraine more broadly, saying “if European security is to come into that question, first we must have a ceasefire, and we must have the basis of a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine.”
“We will have to think this through carefully, together, to ensure that we are stronger in the next decade, than we were in the last.
I think some of what we’ve seen in Europe came at us without us being fully prepared. Not just the aggression, but also the disruption within our democracies and other factors that have sought to weaken Europe.
We will come back stronger in this decade, and we collaborate more deeply on security and defence.”
Asked about British people making up their minds, von der Leyen smiles that “I have many British friends and they are very good at making up their minds.”
“I know that by experience.”
On today’s deals, she backs Burnham’s line that today’s deal matters.
“We have three major agreements where many people thought we would never be able, to come to the finish line.”
“I think, of course, it’s ultimately … for the people of, the UK to decide where the journey goes, to which direction of travel the country is taking.
But I very much welcome, Andy, your willingness to have a broader debate about the future relationship. I can only say we are open for brainstorming, and we welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”
'Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,' Burnham says
Burnham accepts a suggestion from a reporter that “we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship,” as “incremental steps only take us so far.”
“We are in the process of developing a ten year plan for Britain, which will be published next month. It will set out big ambitions about the industrialisation of Britain, getting growth going in all parts of Britain, making Britain a more balanced, more equal country across its regions and nations, and making sure that we do provide new opportunity for young people, new paths into those industries.
So all of those ambitions, in my view, are connected to our long term relationship with our nearest partner and what we will seek to do over the next year, before the next UK EU summit.”
But in a hint of what his future messaging is likely to be, he says:
“The important point is that Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016. Life has moved on in so many ways we couldn’t have imagined, actually; some of the things that have happened in the last decade, not least the issues we were all discussing in the coalition of the Willing in Berlin, yesterday.
So we need to draw a line, … look at the world as it is now, open up a discussion, see what those options are and then allow there to be a process of consideration, as we look towards the next parliament.”
He says “what we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this parliament given what needs to be done to implement it.”
'We draw a line on decade of drift and division by reconnecting with old friends,' Burnham says
Burnham then comes to the conclusion of this speech, echoing the tone of his domestic political messaging:
“Today, we do draw a line on a decade of drift and division by reconnecting with old friends by building a much more constructive relationship with our nearest neighbours and our largest market.
I think people across Britain can look forward now to a better, more hopeful decade ahead of us.”
'Hope is the word,' Burnham says on importance of reset for younger generation
Burnham points to the importance of today’s deal for the UK agriculture sector, saying “we can do something to turn around” the loss of over 30% of exports to the EU in the last decade.
He also talks about migration, saying people’s concerns on this point are being addressed.
But his main message is directed, it seems, at young people as he says:
“So for young people out there who are wondering how this deal today affects them and their lives, I would say: this deal is for you. This deal really is about lifting your life chances.”
He says:
“I think we’re all conscious that the last decade has been hard for many people, but hardest most of all, for the young people of Britain and the young people of the EU.
Brexit did take away opportunity from our young people. It limited their horizons in their lives, but also it was followed by Covid and the impact then was greater as a result of that.”
He says the new deal will offer “a new freedom for anyone under 31” to travel with “much greater ease and ability to travel to any of the wonderful 27 member states to live, to work, to study.”
“Hope is the word,” he says.
He says the UK will introduce a relevant bill into the British parliament to implement today’s deals as early as next week.
'People can see the status quo is not working,' Burnham says
Burnham declares that “this is a good day for Britain, and this is a good day for Europe.”
He says it is “a win-win” for both sides, and, somewhat defensively, stresses that “it is in tune with public opinion in the UK” as latest polling shows Brits favour closer ties with the EU.
“People can see the status quo isn’t working. It’s not good enough for Britain. … They want a better deal than the hard Brexit we ended up with.”
He heavily focuses on the cost of doing business, saying the solutions adopted today “will help take pressure off” and “will help relieved pressure” and “bring the cost of food down.”
He repeats his earlier comments that today’s deal are expected to add 0.5% to UK GDP, “a £17bn boost to the British economy; the single biggest growth measure that we could take in this parliament.”
von der Leyen then turns to SPS deal on foods, which she hails as “a two-way street for our businesses on both sides of the channel” to help with “easier trade, lower costs, and more choice and more affordable food” for consumers.
She also talks about negotiations on linking carbon markets, with further work continuing “towards the UK’s participation in our electricity market.”
She says the two sides also agreed to set up “a dialogue on economic security,” and to work on digital partnership to promote innovation in AI, quantum and secure connectivity in particular.
Like Costa earlier, she also makes a point on security, stressing the continuing support for Ukraine, and on defence and military mobility.
Von der Leyen also talks about joint fight against illegal migration through “a new structured dialogue on migration” to “prevent dangerous crossings and save lives.”
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen is next.
She says “we know the world around us is changing fast, making a close and stronger partnership … the more important.”
She talks about the gradual process of bringing the UK closer again, starting with UK students rejoining Erasmus+ programme from 2027.
She confirms the new mobility scheme will allow “100,000 young people from each side to spend up to three years in each other’s countries to work, to study, to volunteer or simply travel.”
“We both have and respect our own specificities. We in the continent have not adopted the UK’s imperial measurement system – you measure distance in miles and this in kilometres - and we may drive on opposite sides of the road.
But the most important is that we are heading in the same direction, and that is what matters.”

items.title: London private credit firm Northwall Capital sued by e-commerce group

E-commerce brand aggregator Accel Club has alleged in court documents, filed on 9 November, that the Mayfair-based lender unlawfully asked for an immediate [...]
items.body:
London private credit firm Northwall Capital sued by e-commerce group
Private credit firm Northwall Capital is being sued by an e-commerce group in the High Court following a dispute over an $80.7m (£61.6m) loan and the lender’s takeover of the company.
E-commerce brand aggregator Accel Club has alleged in court documents, filed on 9 November, that the Mayfair-based lender unlawfully asked for an immediate payment of the loan before taking control of the firm’s holding companies.
Under the terms of the loan agreement, NorthWall Capital was only permitted to take control of the business’ holding companies if Accel Club was actively ‘in default’ – meaning a formal breach of the debt terms.
Accel Club, which generated around $225m (£172m) in annual revenue in the last year, argued in its filing that Northwall Capital triggered the takeover because of allegedly invalid default notices, including $4.1m (£3.1m) of interest the e-commerce firm claims had already been settled.
Accel Club, which buys and grows third-party brands on Amazon, further argued that the interest had originally been deferred under revised payment terms, claiming it settled the $4.1m (£3.1m) interest payment in July.
The e-commerce group further argues that Northwall Capital acknowledged the receipt of the interest payment in August through its Ireland-based lending vehicle, Denali European Opportunities.
In its argument, it alleges the takeover, which took place in September, amounted to “unlawful enforcement.” It additionally claims it offered to re-pay the loan in full through refinancing prior to the takeover.
NorthWall to ‘vigorously’ defend proceedings
City AM understands that Northwall Capital contends Accel Club was in default for a period of months, according to sources familiar with the matter.
A spokesperson for Northwall Capital said in a statement: “Northwall is aware of the proceedings. They are contrived, meritless and will be defended vigorously.”
The private credit firm is yet to file its defence in the High Court.
Accel Club declined to comment.
