items.title: Fat jabs blow £1bn hole in supermarket sales as demand for alcohol and crisps falls
items.summary: The number of households on weight-loss medications has hit 2.6 million. It means that as many users are now found in British households as vegans and pescatarians combined, according to new research.
items.body:
Fat jabs blow £1bn hole in supermarket sales as demand for alcohol and crisps falls
Fat jabs have shaved over £1billion off Britain's grocery bills as millions of users ditch junk food.
The number of households on weight-loss medications has hit 2.6 million, according to the latest figures from market researchers Worldpanel by Numerator.
It means that as many users are now found in British households as vegans and pescatarians combined.
Analysis shows around one in 12 homes (8.5 per cent) have at least one person taking the appetite-suppressing drugs, three-and-a-half times more than two years ago.
Known as GLP-1s and sold under brand names including Mounjaro and Wegovy, their meteoric rise is having huge implications for food and drink businesses.
The growth of weight loss drugs has hit grocery spend by over £1billion a year, up from £780 million in June – the equivalent of £389 a year from each patient's basket.
Experts at Worldpanel by Numerator have said that weight-loss medications and their use represent 'a seismic change'.
Taken as a weekly injection, the jabs trick the body into thinking it is full, meaning fewer cravings.
The latest figures show 8.5 per cent of households using the medications in August compared with 2.3 per cent in 2024. The proportion has also risen from 6.3 per cent this February.
And now weight loss pills make up 11.2 per cent of GLP-1 users, despite being approved just this summer in the UK, according to the study of 9,629 households.
Chantel Kennaugh, head of public sector and nutrition at Worldpanel by Numberator, said: 'Our estimates suggest that GLP-1 usage is set to surpass 10 per cent of GB households in 2027.
'This is not a flash-in-the pan trend, but a seismic change that requires retailers and manufacturers to re-think their strategies.'
The number of men using the drugs has nearly doubled, now making up 32 per cent of users compared to 23 per cent in February.
Spending on alcohol among the cohort of weight-loss drug users has dropped 15 per cent more compared to households who do not have anyone taking the medication.
Medication such as Mounjaro can make drinking less appealing as it changes how the brain responds to pleasure as well as causing side-effects including feeling sick.
Spending on crisps has also dropped 15 per cent.
Nishita Pattni, senior consultant at Worldpanel by Numerator, said: 'You might see people swapping out three beers for one cocktail.'
But Pattni said some aisles of supermarkets are cashing in as people become more health conscious and want to battle some of the drugs' unwelcome side effects.
These households spent £78 million more than expected on health and beauty products in the first year after adoption, and 30 per cent said they had spent more on clothing and footwear as their bodies changed. Mouthwash is one category that has benefited as users battle issues like dry mouth.
Some categories are even benefiting from users wanting to treat themselves with affordable indulgences because users of the medication - which can cost up to £350 a month - have less disposable income, Pattni said.
This may explain why spending on hot chocolate has gone up, in addition to the drug making users sensitive to stimulants such as coffee. 'Bitesize' versions of chocolates have also risen among this group.
It comes after Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy has said Brits are set to drink less booze this Christmas amid an increased interest in healthy lifestyles. He said he believes there could be a 'more moderate Christmas' when it comes to drinking.

items.title: Worsening Gen-Z sentiment drives consumer confidence lower
items.summary: Gen-Z’s deteriorating financial sentiment is driving a decline in consumer confidence, prompting retailers to urge the government to tackle the cost of living. Falling confidence among young people drove consumer expectations of the UK economy lower in November, according to the British Retail Consortium (BRC).  The cost-of-living crisis is bearing down on British shoppers just [...]
items.body:
Worsening Gen-Z sentiment drives consumer confidence lower
Gen-Z’s deteriorating financial sentiment is driving a decline in consumer confidence, prompting retailers to urge the government to tackle the cost of living.
Falling confidence among young people drove consumer expectations of the UK economy lower in November, according to the British Retail Consortium (BRC).
The cost-of-living crisis is bearing down on British shoppers just as the Christmas shopping season kicks off, in which retailers usually hope for a windfall which gives a boost to their yearly profits.
Consumer confidence fell at its fastest rate since Brexit in October, according to the closely-watched GfK index, and high street bellwether Next revealed a drop-off in spending among UK shoppers last week.
British consumer’s attitudes towards the state of the economy worsened to a net reading of -42 in November, down from -40 in October, according to new data from the BRC and polling firm Opinium.
Shoppers’ opinions about their own financial situation also deteriorated, from -18 in October to -20 this month, the polling found.
The BRC said Brits are bracing to spend more over the Christmas period, reflecting the burden of holiday shopping lists and the anticipation that food prices are soon to rise.
Worsening sentiment among Gen-Z highlights the importance of tackling the youth worklessness crisis, the BRC said, with nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).
Former health secretary Alan Milburn delivered his long-awaited report into youth unemployment on Tuesday, in which he called on the government to cut employment costs and retain a lower minimum wage for young people.
Neets crisis in spotlight
Helen Dickinson, the BRC’s chief executive, said: “Government policies have undermined retailers’ ability to hire by steadily pushing up the costs of employment. Adopting Alan Milburn’s proposal to raise the national insurance threshold for under-25s in retail and hospitality would boost the creation of much-needed entry-level roles for young people.
“Such bold action would allow retailers everywhere to provide meaningful opportunities for young people to take their first step on the career ladder.”
The Food and Drink Federation (FDF) said the grocery sector is spending money keeping the lid on food inflation, which slowed to 0.9 per cent in the year to October, which it would otherwise spend on employing young people.
Liliana Danila, the trade body’s chief economist, said: “While the sector may constrain price rises today, it comes at the cost of delaying crucial investment into new machinery, innovation and jobs or training opportunities for young people.
“That has longer term implications for UK food resilience and these rising costs will eventually be reflected in a higher rate of food inflation.”
Writing in City AM, Pret A Manger chief executive Pano Christou said the government-driven costs facing hospitality are “one of the biggest reasons why young people are struggling to open those doors to good careers”.
Christou, who began his career at Pret as an assistant manager at one of its cafes, said: “Alan Milburn’s report should be the beginning of a bigger rethink. If [the] government wants businesses to employ more young people, they need to reward them for doing it.”

Spanning two levels, the ground floor […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Australian furniture designer, manufacturer and retailer King Living is continuing its UK expansion with the opening of a new 975sq m showroom at Lakeside Retail Park in West Thurrock, Essex, on Saturday 21 November, marking another milestone for the family-owned business as it approaches its 50th anniversary in 2027.
Spanning two levels, the ground floor and mezzanine, the new showroom represents King Living’s continued investment in physical retail and its commitment to bringing contemporary Australian furniture design to more customers across the UK. Situated within an established destination for furniture and home shopping, the Lakeside location will make the brand’s collections more accessible to customers across Essex, East London and the wider South East.
Founded in Sydney in 1977, King Living has grown from an Australian family business into an internationally recognised furniture brand, with a presence across eight countries: Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Canada, the United States, Singapore, Malaysia and China. The company remains family-owned and vertically integrated, developing its collections through its Australian in-house design team and collaborations with leading designers, before manufacturing within its own facilities
The Lakeside opening forms part of King Living’s wider international expansion and reflects the brand’s belief that physical showrooms continue to play an essential role in furniture retail, particularly when customers are making considered purchases intended to last for many years.
Rather than simply displaying furniture, King Living’s showrooms are designed to create an immersive, personalised shopping experience. At Lakeside, customers will be able to explore carefully considered room settings that demonstrate how different collections can work together, while experiencing the comfort, materials and flexibility of the designs firsthand.
Expert guidance will also be available to help customers navigate furniture selection, configurations and finishes, whether they’re investing in an individual piece or furnishing an entire living space. With more than 200 premium fabric and leather options available, personalisation is a key part of the experience, allowing customers to explore different colours, textures and materials to suit their homes.
The new showroom will showcase King Living’s most popular UK sofa collections, including Jasper, 1977, Zaza and Delta, alongside occasional furniture, dining, the King Sleep Collection, outdoor designs, lighting and rugs.
A central part of King Living’s proposition is its approach to designing furniture for longevity. Its sofas incorporate precision-engineered steel frames, backed by a 25-year Steel Frame Warranty, while modular configurations allow customers to adapt their furniture as their living spaces and requirements change. Removable covers and replaceable components also mean designs can be refreshed rather than replaced, extending their useful life.
This philosophy of engineering comfort and longevity into furniture from the outset has been central to King Living’s development over nearly five decades and remains a defining part of its approach to product innovation and customer experience.
As King Living prepares to celebrate its 50th anniversary in 2027, the Lakeside opening represents the next chapter in the brand’s international growth, combining the design and engineering expertise established since 1977 with an ongoing commitment to expanding its physical retail presence.
Should the news of the new opening be of interest for a piece, we can provide supporting imagery and further details, alongside commentary from founder David King on King Living’s continued international expansion, the role of physical showrooms in the furniture retail journey and how five decades of design and engineering are shaping the brand’s next chapter.
Showroom details:
- Opening: Saturday 21 November 2026
- Location: Unit E2, Lakeside Retail Park, West Thurrock Way, West Thurrock, Grays, Essex RM20 1WN
- Size: 975sqm across two levels
- Showroom Manager: Stu Mangan
- Website: https://www.kingliving.co.uk/showroom/lakeside

From today, every pre-order is on its way to customers, and the whisky is pouring in selected bars, restaurants and independent retailers across Wales. items.body:
Hensol Castle Distillery has today officially launched its inaugural Single Malt Welsh Whisky, the first whisky to be distilled and matured at the historic estate. From today, every pre-order is on its way to customers, and the whisky is pouring in selected bars, restaurants and independent retailers across Wales.
The launch marks a landmark moment for the award-winning South Wales distillery and a new arrival in the fast-growing Single Malt Welsh Whisky category.
Grain to glass, under one roof
The whisky programme began in 2022, and on 27 February 2023 the distillery team filled “Barrel No.1”, the first cask of the inaugural edition. Every step since has been carried out at Hensol. The process starts with a 100% malted barley wash, developed with partners at Newport’s Tiny Rebel Brewery. The spirit is then distilled on-site and matured in the castle’s cellars.
After more than three and a half years in premium American bourbon barrels, the result is a rich, remarkably complex spirit for its age and well-balanced Welsh single malt with notes of orchard fruit, penny toffee and honeyed oak.
“Starting our journey into the whisky world wasn’t something we took lightly; whisky is a decision for the future, a legacy,” said Kyle Jones, Master Distiller at Hensol Castle Distillery. “Our goal was to craft a liquid as timeless as the castle itself, while putting our own stamp on a thriving Welsh whisky category. With precision, expertise and a quiet obsession for the craft, I can confidently say we have exceeded that goal.”
“Filling that first barrel back in 2023 wasn’t about noise or chasing headlines; it was about starting something properly,” Jones added. “Welsh whisky has a proud heritage, and we wanted to respect that from day one. It’s ready, it’s distinct, and it’s everything we hoped it would be.”
A strictly limited first release
The first run is limited to just over 1,000 bottles:
- 500 bottles were set aside for the distillery’s direct-to-consumer community through pre-orders, which opened at the end of September. All pre-orders are dispatched today.
- 500 bottles have gone to Welsh on-trade partners, selected independent retailers and two wholesalers: Fine Wines Direct (National and South Wales) and Blas ar Fwyd (National and North Wales).
Backing Welsh hospitality
To recognise what the Welsh hospitality sector brings to the drinks industry, Hensol Castle has partnered with several of Wales’s top bars for the launch. The distillery has put together a map of venues where drinkers can try a dram of the first release while supporting local hospitality. follow out socials for where to grab your dram.
To mark the release, Hensol Castle Distillery is hosting a press and invited-guest event at the castle and distillery on December 3rd 2026
A new Master Distiller for a new chapter
The launch is also the first release under Kyle Jones, who was recently appointed Master Distiller. Jones has worked on the single malt programme since its earliest planning stages in 2022, alongside former Master Distiller and Head of Commercial Dai Wakely. After five years with the business, Wakely stepped down at the end of September and will continue working with Hensol as a consultant. With the first batch released, Jones now takes full responsibility for the whisky programme and its future development.
What comes next
The distillery is already planning future releases. The team recently made an 1,800-mile round trip to Bordeaux to inspect and select barrels in person, securing 12 finishing casks for a pipeline of highly limited-edition releases in the coming years.
“We are thrilled to be adding our first single malt to the vibrant Single Malt Welsh Whisky category,” said Nate Sorby, Head of Marketing at Hensol Castle Distillery. “The growth and reputation of Welsh spirits over recent years has been incredible to watch, and as an award-winning distillery in the heart of South Wales, we’re proud to play a role in that momentum. Today’s launch is a key milestone as we establish Hensol Castle as a premier, quality-led spirits house, and it’s only the beginning.”
Hensol Castle Single Malt Welsh Whisky is available now from HCD website and at partner venues and retailers across Wales while stocks last.

Sara Bennison has been appointed chair of the John Lewis Partnership Foundation as the charity enters its 20th year. Established in 2007, the Foundation supports charities and community organisations helping people develop skills and overcome barriers to employment, particularly those […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Sara Bennison has been appointed chair of the John Lewis Partnership Foundation as the charity enters its 20th year.
Sara succeeds Dame Oriana Clare Tickell, who will complete the transition by the new year. Established in 2007, the Foundation supports charities and community organisations helping people develop skills and overcome barriers to employment, particularly those with experience of care. It also supports projects to protect and restore the natural environment.
Over the past five years alone, the Foundation has awarded more than £7m to good causes, including £600,000 this year to organisations helping people into work. It also draws on the skills of John Lewis and Waitrose Partners (employees) through its Golden Jubilee Trust, which has enabled more than 1,150 Partners to share their time and expertise with charities since 2000.
Sara brings more than 15 years of non-profit trustee experience, alongside a successful executive career. She served for 10 years as a Trustee of The Prince’s (now Royal) Countryside Fund and spent five years as a Trustee of the Nationwide Foundation. Sara has also held Executive Committee roles at Barclays and Nationwide Building Society, and holds a non-executive portfolio, serving on the boards of The West Brom Building Society, The Openwork Partnership and Equifax.
Nina Bhatia, Managing Director, New Businesses at John Lewis Partnership, said: “Our purpose is to work towards a happier world, and the Foundation plays an important part in bringing that to life. As we enter its 20th year, we want to build on the Foundation’s achievements and ensure its work makes the greatest possible impact, working closely with the wider Partnership. Sara brings a wealth of experience across the charitable and business sectors to help us achieve that.
“I’d like to thank Dame Clare for her invaluable contribution and leadership of the Foundation. Clare has played a pivotal role in the development of the Foundation, for which we’re incredibly grateful, and we wish her all the best for the future.”
Sara Bennison said: “It is a huge privilege to be asked to Chair the John Lewis Partnership Foundation. I very much look forward to working with the team and on projects where our support will make a difference, and that in turn makes our Partners proud.”
Dame Clare Tickell said: “It has been a great pleasure working with the Trustees, the Partnership and the team to build a new and exciting vision for the Foundation. Sara’s experience and ambition make her a perfect fit, and the Foundation is in very safe hands. I will watch with interest and pride as it goes from strength to strength.”

items.title: UK retailers admit gaps in keeping shoppers safe, as government urges UK to ‘Be Ready’
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Millions of UK consumers are about to share their personal data with retailers at scale as the festive season gets underway with Black Friday. Yet UK retailers are prioritising investment in customer experience and AI over cyber security, with only 9% claiming to be ahead on keeping customers safe, according to research commissioned by ecommerce […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Millions of UK consumers are about to share their personal data with retailers at scale as the festive season gets underway with Black Friday. Yet UK retailers are prioritising investment in customer experience and AI over cyber security, with only 9% claiming to be ahead on keeping customers safe, according to research commissioned by ecommerce agency Quickfire Digital.
Overwhelmingly, 86% acknowledge at least one area to improve including crisis response (37%), website accessibility (33%), data privacy regulations and compliance (33%) and cyber security (28%), which is a concern when last year £11.8m was lost to online shopping fraud.
The findings come as the UK government’s Be Ready campaign launched last month (October 2026) asking households to prepare for disruption from emergencies. The Defence Secretary added that the country needed to ask businesses whether they were prepared for increasingly sophisticated cyber attacks.
A survey of over 2,000 UK adults, carried alongside a survey of 206 UK ecommerce retailers in August 2026 found that these gaps in preparedness coincide with plans that depend on customer data and trust.
AI and personalisation are retailers’ top investment priorities for the year ahead, both strategies depending on collecting and using customer data effectively. Being transparent about how they use customer data remains a challenge for nearly a quarter of UK retailers (22%) and a further 15% identify data security and trust as an area of their business not currently delivering a good customer experience. This matters as in June this year retailers became legally required to give customers a clear way to raise a data protection complaint, and to respond within 30 days.
For shoppers, trust is part of the retail experience and they already have reservations about the personalised features that rely most on their data. Only 17% say they like product recommendations tailored to them, down from 24% a year earlier, and 13% like tailored offers or notifications, down from 20%.
Asked what would encourage them to become loyal to a brand, just 2% chose personalised recommendations, while 15% say a lack of trust in a brand would most likely make them abandon an online purchase.
Martin Harper, co-founder of Quickfire Digital, commented: “Retailers have been very candid here, and that is useful when it comes to both protecting consumers and advancing the retail industry. Every gap they have identified, from how they respond when something goes wrong to whether their website works for every customer, can be fixed, and most without new technology.
“Data is at the centre of how retailers compete. Personalised experiences, smarter recommendations, better forecasting – none of this works without customers choosing to share their data, and people only share with businesses they trust. Retailers that have plans in place to how they will respond when things go wrong, make their sites accessible and explain in plain English what they collect and why, will be in a far stronger position to ask for more. Ultimately this is the best way to get real value from the data they already hold.”
The findings are taken from The State of Ecommerce 2026, Quickfire Digital’s annual report on the health of UK ecommerce, published on 12 October 2026. The report compares 2025 and 2026 retailer and consumer data and includes contributions from 19+ industry experts and is available at https://www.quickfiredigital.com/white-papers/the-state-of-ecommerce-2026/

items.title: JD Sports’ recovery remains slow as core fascia continues to struggle, says GlobalData

Following today’s release of JD Sports’s figures for the three months months ending 31 October 2026; Louise Deglise-Favre, lead apparel analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “JD Sports’ performance in Q3 FY2026/27 showed only the faintest sign of stabilisation, with organic sales down 1.1%, a marginal improvement on Q2 […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Following today’s release of JD Sports’s figures for the three months months ending 31 October 2026; Louise Deglise-Favre, lead apparel analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “JD Sports’ performance in Q3 FY2026/27 showed only the faintest sign of stabilisation, with organic sales down 1.1%, a marginal improvement on Q2 that owes more to favourable timing of Back-to-School in North America, than to a genuine pick-up in demand. Although JD Sports’ stated trading was in line with expectations, it now expects FY2026/27 profit before tax and adjusting items in the range of £700m-£750m, down from £700m-£800m. While presented as a ‘narrowing’, lowering the top end of the range points to a more cautious outlook for the year, and with sales still supported by promotions and new space, a sustained recovery in underlying trading may take a little longer to come through.
“The core JD fascia remained under pressure, with organic sales down 1.6% and l-f-l sales falling 3.7%, as lower store footfall and heightened promotional activity in North America during the Finish Line conversion weighed on established stores. The JD fascia continued to be hindered by a soft footwear performance too due in part to aging Nike product lines, on which JD Sports remains reliant, and a highly promotional market environment. Growth in performance running and seasonal fashion lines is encouraging but not yet enough to offset this. While the warmer weather at the beginning of the quarter delayed demand for autumn/winter apparel, its inadequate footwear offering has undoubtedly had a bigger impact on the fascia’s sales performance. Complementary Athleisure continued to struggle, posting an organic decline of 3.3% amid heavy promotional activity. The Sporting Goods & Outdoor segment was again the group’s star performer, with organic sales up 6.2% and l-f-l sales increasing 5.1%, driven by refreshed ranges and resilient demand for technical products.
“North America showed the clearest improvement, with l-f-l sales down 2.2% and organic sales growing 0.5%, although this was flattered by Back-to-School demand shifting from July into August. In Europe, l-f-l sales fell 2.7% and organic sales slipped 0.9%, with soft footwear and civil unrest in France weighing on trading. The UK was the weakest region on an organic basis, falling 4.2%, with l-f-l sales down 2.6%, as the World Cup boost to Q2 faded and net store closures shrank the estate. Asia Pacific, previously the group’s best-performing region, slowed sharply, with l-f-l sales falling 5.3% and organic sales rising just 2.3%, suggesting growth there now relies almost entirely on new space.”

A focus on improving customer experience with design-led products and partnerships with leading international stationery brands has been rewarded with improved margins that helped to successfully drive the […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
High Street Stationer Ryman delivered an EBITDA of £3.3m on turnover of £102.2m for the year ended March 2026, against a £1.6m EBITDA in the prior year.
A focus on improving customer experience with design-led products and partnerships with leading international stationery brands has been rewarded with improved margins that helped to successfully drive the bottom line. Store sales were ahead of plan (+0.2% like-for-like), resulting from success in the strategy to focus growth on stationery related products and services, countering declines in higher priced, lower margin categories such as printers and ink. This validated our new future-proofing business strategy, confirming Ryman’s reason to exist on the high street, whilst also attracting a younger more fashion-conscious consumer customer.
A full review of the e-commerce channel also saw improved profitability coming from lower sales, providing a solid base for pushing this channel on. The strategy has been endorsed further by the customer base with profitability across both channels improving further in the current year with sales and profit well ahead of 2026, which is expected to continue.
Ryman has invested in developing the store portfolio, including new Ryman Design stores with Bluewater opening in July 2026, new concept stores in Victoria and Kensington London, Harrow, Sutton Coldfield, Durham, as well as refurbishments to existing stores including Manchester Arndale. Further opportunities are being explored for both Ryman and Ryman Design as well as extending the partnership with the Post Office, where new locations become available.
As well as partnerships with new brands, Ryman improved its proposition to customers by enhancing its click-and-collect service and partnering with Deliveroo to provide an express delivery service through its nationwide network of stores.
Theo Paphitis, Chair and Owner of Ryman said: “I am delighted with the progress made by Ryman in the last year, which has continued into the current year. The change in our customers’ daily habits, in their work and study following the pandemic, meant we needed to reposition Ryman giving it a renewed reason to exist and prosper again. Everything changed in 2020, despite Ryman having an over 130 year history and delivering sustainable profits during my ownership of 30 years. In response, the management team and I have worked tirelessly, and collaborated with our existing and new partners, to make Ryman relevant for the current and future customer.
We have driven countless initiatives which, together with a sharp focus on profitable activities, have seen Ryman’s profits build again. UK retail is in no doubt challenging, however, I have backed my businesses throughout and stayed focused on having a reason to exist. I now look forward to an exciting future for Ryman.
As well as my support, our bankers, NatWest, have agreed to extend facilities to 2030, which allows us to continue to develop our existing business as well as pursue many more exciting opportunities.
Customer appetites for exciting stationery are strong, and there is much to look forward to with further like-for-like growth to date this year, along with increased margins and a further growth in profits.”

items.title: Asda eyes takeover of discount chain amid supermarket merger talks
items.summary: Asda is exploring possible acquisitions, with B&M, The Range and Home Bargains among the businesses that could reportedly be a good fit. Sources close to Asda said a merger with…
items.body:
Asda eyes takeover of discount chain amid supermarket merger talks
Asda is exploring possible acquisitions, with B&M, The Range and Home Bargains among the businesses that could reportedly be a good fit.
Sources close to Asda said a merger with another major supermarket had not been ruled out, although a deal with a business outside the grocery sector was considered more likely.
The discussions are still at an early stage, with any significant acquisition potentially several years away as Asda works to improve its financial position.
The decision follows the appointment of former Morrisons boss David Potts as chief executive earlier this month, as the struggling company looks to win back customers and reverse years of falling market share.
As previously reported, Potts took over from Allan Leighton on 3 November, with the former Asda boss moving into a non-executive chairman role.
Potts, who led Morrisons for eight years and previously spent almost four decades at Tesco, has been tasked with improving the supermarket’s performance after a difficult period under private equity ownership.
The potential dealmaking has come to light as Britain’s supermarket industry faces renewed speculation over consolidation.
Last month, it emerged that Sainsbury’s had held talks with Morrisons over a multibillion-pound merger that would have created a grocery group with almost a quarter of the UK market.
Although those discussions ended earlier this year, a future agreement has not been ruled out.
Asda could also look to acquire stores that may need to be sold if a deal between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons were to go ahead.
Any major supermarket merger would face scrutiny from the Competition and Markets Authority, which blocked Sainsbury’s proposed £7.3bn takeover of Asda in 2019 over concerns about higher prices and reduced competition.
However, the rapid growth of Aldi and Lidl has changed the competitive landscape considerably since then.
Asda’s interest in acquisitions comes despite its own continued trading difficulties.
The supermarket was the only major UK grocer to report falling sales in the latest Worldpanel figures, with sales slipping 0.5 per cent in the 12 weeks to 1 November.
Its market share also fell from 11.6 per cent to 11.3 per cent, as reported last week.

items.title: Tesco shoppers could win £1,000 for local charities in new fundraising drive
items.summary: Tesco shoppers have until 30 November to help their favourite charity, school or community group win £1,000, as it joins forces with easyfundraising ahead of Christmas. The company has teamed…
items.body:
Tesco shoppers could win £1,000 for local charities in new fundraising drive
Tesco shoppers have until 30 November to help their favourite charity, school or community group win £1,000, as it joins forces with easyfundraising ahead of Christmas.
The company has teamed up with the fundraising platform for a November campaign that will see one shopper secure a £1,000 donation for their chosen cause, alongside a £100 Tesco gift card for themselves.
To enter, customers must spend more than £80 in a single transaction at a Tesco store using a bank card linked to their easyfundraising account.
Shoppers need to register through the easyfundraising app, choose a charity or community organisation to support and link their payment card before making a qualifying purchase.
Each eligible shop will count as an entry into the prize draw, which closes on Monday 30 November.
The partnership also allows shoppers to raise money for their chosen cause through qualifying Tesco purchases without paying anything extra.
The initiative is open to a wide range of organisations, including schools, nurseries, sports clubs, charities, community groups and not-for-profit organisations.
Easyfundraising chief executive James Moir said: “With Christmas approaching, we know that every pound counts for local charities, schools and community groups. A £1,000 funding boost could help pay for everything from new equipment and activities to heating and essential running costs.”
He added that linking a payment card allows shoppers to raise funds through purchases they were already planning to make.
The campaign builds on Tesco’s wider community work.
To date, Tesco’s Free Fruit & Veg for Schools programme has distributed almost 20 million portions to pupils, with the scheme expanding to more than 1,000 schools.
Meanwhile, Tesco’s partnership with In Kind Direct has helped distribute more than six million essential hygiene products to families in need.
Since launching in 2007, easyfundraising has helped raise more than £72m for good causes, with over 190,000 organisations registered on its platform and more than two million shoppers using the service.
The fundraising platform has also introduced gift cards across more than 300 brands, allowing shoppers to generate donations when buying vouchers for themselves or others.
Customers can enter the Tesco draw through easyfundraising’s November campaign until 11.59pm on 30 November.

items.title: Tesco, Asda and M&S back IGD sustainability scheme as 326 food businesses engage
items.summary: More than 326 UK food businesses including Tesco, Asda and M&S have engaged with IGD’s Food Supply Chain Sustainability Framework in its first year. The scheme, launched in November 2025,…
items.body:
Tesco, Asda and M&S back IGD sustainability scheme as 326 food businesses engage
More than 326 UK food businesses including Tesco, Asda and M&S have engaged with IGD’s Food Supply Chain Sustainability Framework in its first year.
The scheme, launched in November 2025, has attracted support from 18 major businesses, including the likes of Waitrose, Co-op and Ocado Retail, in addition to the businesses named above.
Food manufacturers including Greencore, Premier Foods, Princes and PepsiCo have also backed the initiative, which aims to make it easier for businesses and their suppliers to work together on sustainability targets.
IGD said engagement over the past year has ranged from companies reviewing the framework and sharing it with suppliers to running pilots, training procurement teams and incorporating its guidance into existing policies.
The framework covers seven sustainability priorities, helping businesses identify where they can make improvements and agree on practical steps with suppliers.
The update comes as food businesses grapple with rising costs, extreme weather and growing uncertainty over the availability of key ingredients.
As previously reported, separate IGD research found that 91 per cent of food industry leaders and academics believe risks to the UK food system have increased over the past year.
To help businesses put the framework into practice, IGD has launched a new guide aimed at sustainability, procurement and commercial teams.
It sets out how companies can identify priority suppliers, assess their progress and agree on actions that can be built into everyday buying decisions.
Earlier this week, Tesco launched a new Climate Supplier Programme to help its UK suppliers cut emissions, as part of its ambition to reach net zero across its value chain by 2050.
Meanwhile, Waitrose recently signed a global initiative to support regenerative farming, following a year of extreme weather that has put pressure on British food production.
Greencore climate lead Zoe Mountford said the IGD framework was helping the manufacturer have more focused discussions with its customers and suppliers.
“We’ve also built key elements into our Supplier Code of Conduct, helping us focus on the most material priorities and turn those conversations into practical action,” she said.
IGD is now working towards wider adoption of the framework through a roadmap running to 2030.
It also plans to introduce a digital version in the coming months, allowing businesses to complete assessments and track their progress more easily.
However, the first-year figures reflect varying levels of engagement, rather than 326 businesses having fully implemented the scheme or achieved measurable reductions in emissions.

items.title: John Lewis Partnership Foundation appoints Sara Bennison as chair
items.summary: The John Lewis Partnership Foundation has appointed Sara Bennison as its new chair as the charity prepares to mark its 20th anniversary. Bennison takes over from Dame Clare Tickell, who will complete the handover by the new year, bringing more than 15 years of experience as a charity trustee alongside a career in financial services....
items.body:
The John Lewis Partnership Foundation has appointed Sara Bennison as its new chair as the charity prepares to mark its 20th anniversary.
Bennison takes over from Dame Clare Tickell, who will complete the handover by the new year, bringing more than 15 years of experience as a charity trustee alongside a career in financial services.
She previously spent a decade as a trustee of The Prince’s (now Royal) Countryside Fund and five years at the Nationwide Foundation, as well as holding senior roles at Barclays and Nationwide Building Society.
Bennison also sits on the boards of The West Brom Building Society, The Openwork Partnership and Equifax.
Established in 2007, the John Lewis Partnership Foundation supports charities helping people overcome barriers to employment, particularly those who have spent time in care, alongside projects focused on protecting the environment.
The charity has awarded more than £7m to good causes over the past five years, including £600,000 this year to organisations helping people into work.
It also runs the Golden Jubilee Trust, which has enabled more than 1,150 John Lewis and Waitrose employees to volunteer their skills and expertise with charities since 2000.
The appointment comes as the Partnership continues to expand its support for care-experienced young people.
As reported in June, John Lewis pledged to create another 1,000 job opportunities for young people leaving care, building on its existing employment initiatives.
The business also revealed last year that it had raised almost £3m for charities supporting care-experienced young peoplethrough its Building Happier Futures programme.
John Lewis Partnership managing director of new businesses Nina Bhatia said: “As we enter its 20th year, we want to build on the Foundation’s achievements and ensure its work makes the greatest possible impact, working closely with the wider Partnership.”
She added that Bennison’s experience across the charity and business sectors would help the Foundation build on its work.
Bennison said: “It is a huge privilege to be asked to Chair the John Lewis Partnership Foundation. I very much look forward to working with the team and on projects where our support will make a difference, and that in turn makes our Partners proud.”
Outgoing chair Dame Clare Tickell said Bennison’s experience and ambition made her a strong fit for the role, adding that the Foundation was in “very safe hands”.

items.title: Is Poundland’s public and political attention creating a poisoned chalice?
items.summary: Poundland has about 600 shops, a management team that says it has brought the business back into profit and a prospective buyer prepared to take the whole thing on. It also has until 26 November before its latest protection from creditors expires. For the staff who gathered outside its Walsall headquarters last month, the bit...
items.body:
Poundland has about 600 shops, a management team that says it has brought the business back into profit and a prospective buyer prepared to take the whole thing on.
It also has until 26 November before its latest protection from creditors expires. For the staff who gathered outside its Walsall headquarters last month, the bit that needed explaining was how all these things could be true at once.
It’s the possibility of a break-up, when there appears to be an alternative, that has made Poundland’s sale a matter for parliament. Workers have protested, the prime minister has intervened and MPs have called in the European boss of Gordon Brothers, the American investment firm that bought the chain for £1 last year.
In the Commons, the Conservative MP Bradley Thomas asked a question with rather more bearing on the lives of his constituents than most of the speculation about bidders: “If individual stores are sold, will their employees keep their jobs?”
Much of the anger concerns an offer from Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group. Poundland’s management backed it. According to Sky News, it failed to progress because it would repay too little of a £22.5m loan owed to Gordon Brothers.
The owner says it has provided £85m in financing, prefers a sale of the whole business and wants a buyer with the means to keep trading. There are two sums of money at issue here. One is what Poundland needs from a new owner. The other is what its present owner wants out. It seems fair, with thousands of livelihoods at stake, to ask which sum is proving the greater obstacle.
The staff have a particular claim to an answer; around 150 shops have already closed since summer 2025. At the remaining stores, customers have responded to the return of a recognisable Poundland proposition, with half the grocery range priced at £1.
Green shoots, but challenges persist
Like-for-like sales rose 3.3 per cent in the quarter to 27 September, and managing director Barry Williams told staff that annual earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation had reached £18.1m, against a £68.1m loss a year earlier.
Anyone who worked through that and then found themselves outside head office chanting “save our jobs” might reasonably wonder whose turn it was to make a concession.
A buyer looking at those same figures might reasonably ask how a company making £18.1m had lately found itself struggling to order Yorkshire Tea. The answer matters more to its prospects than another week of speculation about the sale price.
Someone has to advance the cash for the tea before a shopper pays for it. This month, as MPs pressed Gordon Brothers over funding, money became available to place orders and more than 50 suppliers sent goods to Poundland’s depots.
‘Political risk and inflammatory commentary’
Yet consider how the past few weeks might look from Denmark. Salling Group, which owns Netto, reportedly withdrew from the process after its representatives cited “political risk and inflammatory commentary”, according to a City source quoted by The Telegraph.
It would be quite a leap from one source’s account to blaming MPs for the loss of a viable deal. Still, Salling knows the British discount market. When its 16-store venture with Sainsbury’s ended in 2016, one difficulty the partners identified was the cost of acquiring enough sites quickly enough. An estate the size of Poundland’s ought at least to have been worth a second look.
What has changed is what it would mean, publicly, to buy those shops. A bidder can undertake to acquire Poundland as a going concern. An employee hearing that their job has been saved is likely to understand something more enduring. The two interpretations can coexist quite happily until the first lease comes up for renewal.
At that point, a decision the buyer thought it was entitled to make on the rent may look, to everyone else, like a promise broken.
Gordon Brothers says it has also received offers for substantial parts of the estate. Those bidders enjoy an advantage. They can tell workers in the shops they take on what they intend to do for them. Nobody expects them to visit the towns they passed over.
Buy Poundland whole, however, and every town is yours to answer to. The staff in Walsall had good reason to make a public cause of keeping the chain together. What should perhaps trouble them is how much easier it would be for a buyer to defend taking it apart.

items.title: Complex products need expert advice – cutting staff investment puts that at risk
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. By Daniel Todaro, CEO at Gekko Group With increasing overheads, a growing tax burden and changing employment laws, retailers are understandably cutting headcount in favour of AI and technology-enabled services. At a time when many retailers, particularly those with a physical presence, are under pressure this is a rational decision but there are some significant […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
By Daniel Todaro, CEO at Gekko Group
With increasing overheads, a growing tax burden and changing employment laws, retailers are understandably cutting headcount in favour of AI and technology-enabled services. At a time when many retailers, particularly those with a physical presence, are under pressure this is a rational decision but there are some significant drawbacks that are being overlooked – and it could come back to haunt them.
Physical retail still plays a vital role in the customer journey
Outside of the Black Friday rush, three quarters of purchases are still made in store, despite growing web traffic. The increase of webrooming – where consumers browse online before making a purchase in-store – and showrooming, where the opposite is true, highlights the need for consistent, high-quality experiences across channels.
Consumers often prefer to see a product in person before they commit to a purchase – even if that purchase is ultimately made online. This is particularly true of big-ticket items such as technology, white goods and furniture where shoppers want to know exactly what they are getting before they part with their money – especially so in today’s market where many single people and families are feeling squeezed financially.
It is easy to assume that simply having trial or sample products available meets these needs, but there is an additional layer that is often being forgotten: advice. Consumers have reviews and product information at their fingertips, but sometimes they want to discuss their prospective purchases with someone in the know and that is where staffing matters.
When shoppers go into a store and cannot find anyone to assist them, it detracts from the experience and often causes them to either abandon their purchase or feel undervalued, which can often damage their perception of the retailer or brand.
Information is no substitute for experience and expertise
Experienced and well-trained staffing becomes even more important when it comes to complex products. Let’s say you are in the market for a new wearable, a fitness tracker for example: there are an overwhelming volume of options available – brand, model, specification, price point. The discovery process is exhausting and it’s difficult to tell the difference between products, especially with limited technical knowledge and expertise.
Your friends have told you what they have and you might know that you want a ring over a watch or band, but beyond that it can be a slog. Which model works for you and your lifestyle: top of the range or will a less expensive version meet your needs? You have done your research but the information available is confusing and conflicted, so you decide to go into a store to try out some options and speak to an expert who can help you make the decision, but it takes you a long time to find a member of staff, and when you do, they often can’t provide the kind of expert advice and genuine user experience that you’re after..
Here the issue is not only headcount, but expertise. When it comes to big-ticket items, retailers and brands must be equipped to convert confusion into action. Training budgets are being cut to reduce overheads, with in-person practical training being replaced by online learning. Digital updates provide a solid foundation, but surface-level modules do not inspire teams’ confidence or build their ability to sell more complex products and services. As tech products – wearables, laptops, mobile phones, white goods and even small domestic appliances – become increasingly complex and more confusing for the average shopper, the need for in-depth knowledge is becoming a necessity rather than a nice to have to avoid buyers’ remorse.
Brands with more complicated products should consider placing brand ambassadors in store or providing additional training to stockists’ staff to ensure that someone is on hand to answer challenging questions, reassure shoppers and help them find the model that will strike the best balance between their needs and their budget. This high-quality experience engenders trust and brand equity, which is vital for long-term commercial success as the cost of ambassadors outweighs the potential failure and delisting of a brand and its products. If standards slip, and sales are low, it can have a sizeable impact on the bottom line.
Overreliance on AI can be detrimental
In-store staffing and expertise is essential, but the experience needs to be consistent across touchpoints. With consumers increasingly browsing or researching products online, product labelling, descriptions, images and tags must be accurate to be discoverable, accessible and comparable. Digital shelf management is one area where automated services and AI can be incredibly valuable – but when it comes to the wider customer experience, the overreliance on technology is letting many brands and retailers down.
Customer service is a vital part of the customer journey. While much of this has moved online, chatbots are rapidly becoming a replacement for human interactions as retailers take advantage of technology to reduce overheads. However, 83% of consumers still prefer to speak to a real person, and frustrating experiences with automated services are impacting the customer experience – and that’s costing businesses. Everyone knows when they are talking to a chatbot. If you want to make your customer feel valued, this isn’t going to achieve it.
A study from CEBR and Trustpilot published in October last year revealed that poor experiences with AI may have cost UK retail firms as much as £8.6bn in the previous 12 months – and with the industry already in a bind, this is a loss few retailers can afford. This shows the importance of having empathetic, expert staff available: even if a chatbot is the first point of contact, there is value in making the path to human interaction straightforward and allowing consumers to engage in a way that suits them.
In-store or online, human experience is the new premium
As AI interactions often disappoint and access to in-store support becomes limited, the human touch has become a rarity. Most consumers are prepared to pay more for better customer service, and as more retailers reduce their headcounts, being able to engage with real people – online and face-to-face – will be perceived as a premium experience.
This is particularly important for those selling those complex, big-ticket items. Customer experience should match the price point, and failing to deliver what shoppers want and need only fosters a feeling of dissatisfaction.

items.title: Tesco parcel lockers drive repeat visits as network reaches 1,650
items.summary: More than half of shoppers using InPost lockers at Tesco say they now visit the supermarket more often, prompting further expansion across its estate. New figures from InPost show that 53 per cent of its locker users say the service encourages them to visit Tesco more frequently, while 66 per cent combine collecting or returning...
items.body:
More than half of shoppers using InPost lockers at Tesco say they now visit the supermarket more often, prompting further expansion across its estate.
New figures from InPost show that 53 per cent of its locker users say the service encourages them to visit Tesco more frequently, while 66 per cent combine collecting or returning a parcel with a grocery shop.
Tesco has reached 1,650 InPost lockers across its UK estate, making it the delivery firm’s largest single retail partner network in the country.
The partnership, which began in 2021, now covers Tesco’s different store formats, from Express convenience shops to larger Extra and Superstore locations.
InPost’s research, conducted with Tesco between January and September 2025, also found that 75 per cent of locker users felt the service made their shopping trip more convenient.
However, the figures are based on customer responses rather than independently measured changes in store footfall or spending.
Tesco head of property income Nick Burrows said: “We’re always looking for ways to make the shopping trip more convenient for customers.”
He added that the growing locker network allows customers to collect, send and return parcels while carrying out their everyday shopping.
The milestone follows Tesco’s efforts to bring more delivery services into its stores.
As reported in March, Tesco began trialling Evri-branded lockers at selected Extra and Superstore locations, bringing different parcel providers together under one roof.
The trial builds on its existing relationship with Evri, which also allows Clubcard members to earn points when sending parcels through the delivery company.
Tesco is not alone in making more space for parcel collections and returns.
Earlier this year, Morrisons expanded its parcel locker partnership with Quadient, with plans to bring the service to 500 supermarkets across the UK.
The growing investment comes as more shoppers turn to lockers rather than relying on home deliveries.
As Retail Gazette explored earlier this year, parcel lockers are becoming an increasingly important part of the shopping experience, offering businesses a way to attract visits while giving customers more flexibility over deliveries and returns.

items.body:
Asos has become the first wholesale partner for Millie Bobby Brown’s Florence by Mills fashion brand in the UK and Europe.
The collection, which launched on 17 November, features 32 pieces spanning everyday basics, loungewear, pyjamas, dresses and matching sets.
Among the products are the brand’s Signature Softie Cotton and seamless essentials, après-ski-inspired sets and festive nightwear.
The launch marks Florence by Mills fashion’s first wholesale partnership across the UK and EU, with the range available to customers across all Asos markets.
Founded by the Stranger Things actress in 2019 as a beauty and lifestyle brand, Florence by Mills expanded into clothing in 2024, with a focus on comfortable, accessible fashion aimed at younger consumers.
Asos partner brands director Bernadette Sullivan said: “We’re thrilled to welcome Florence by Mills fashion to Asos and to become the brand’s first wholesale partner in the UK and EU.”
She added that the brand’s accessible price points and focus on comfort and self-expression would appeal to Asos shoppers, while introducing Florence by Mills to new audiences.
Asos is continuing to push on broadening its third-party brand offering.
Earlier this year, Asos expanded its menswear portfolio with nine new brands, including Gap. The latest addition also follows a return to growth for Asos, which has spent the past few years working to turn around its performance.
As reported earlier this month, Asos swung to a £24.4m pre-tax profit and recorded quarterly sales growth for the first time since 2022.
The business has also been leaning further into celebrity partnerships and fashion-led campaigns to reconnect with younger shoppers, as explored in Retail Gazette’s recent look at how Asos, M&S and Topshop are refreshing their appeal.

items.title: Asda eyes takeover of discount chain amid supermarket merger talks
items.summary: Asda is exploring possible acquisitions, with B&M, The Range and Home Bargains among the businesses that could reportedly be a good fit. Sources close to Asda said a merger with another major supermarket had not been ruled out, although a deal with a business outside the grocery sector was considered more likely. The discussions are...
items.body:
Asda is exploring possible acquisitions, with B&M, The Range and Home Bargains among the businesses that could reportedly be a good fit.
Sources close to Asda said a merger with another major supermarket had not been ruled out, although a deal with a business outside the grocery sector was considered more likely.
The discussions are still at an early stage, with any significant acquisition potentially several years away as Asda works to improve its financial position.
The decision follows the appointment of former Morrisons boss David Potts as chief executive earlier this month, as the struggling company looks to win back customers and reverse years of falling market share.
As previously reported, Potts took over from Allan Leighton on 3 November, with the former Asda boss moving into a non-executive chairman role.
Potts, who led Morrisons for eight years and previously spent almost four decades at Tesco, has been tasked with improving the supermarket’s performance after a difficult period under private equity ownership.
The potential dealmaking has come to light as Britain’s supermarket industry faces renewed speculation over consolidation.
Last month, it emerged that Sainsbury’s had held talks with Morrisons over a multibillion-pound merger that would have created a grocery group with almost a quarter of the UK market.
Although those discussions ended earlier this year, a future agreement has not been ruled out.
Asda could also look to acquire stores that may need to be sold if a deal between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons were to go ahead.
Any major supermarket merger would face scrutiny from the Competition and Markets Authority, which blocked Sainsbury’s proposed £7.3bn takeover of Asda in 2019 over concerns about higher prices and reduced competition.
However, the rapid growth of Aldi and Lidl has changed the competitive landscape considerably since then.
Asda’s interest in acquisitions comes despite its own continued trading difficulties.
The supermarket was the only major UK grocer to report falling sales in the latest Worldpanel figures, with sales slipping 0.5 per cent in the 12 weeks to 1 November.
Its market share also fell from 11.6 per cent to 11.3 per cent, as reported last week.

items.body:
Alibaba.com, a global business-to-business (B2B) e-commerce platform, has today launched its “European SME Startup Pack”, opening free access to Accio Sourcing Expert in Auto Mode for small and medium-sized businesses (SMEs) across Europe. Announced at the opening of its two-day CoCreate Europe summit at Excel London (19–20 November), the new pack bundles cost-effective sourcing and design tools, and automates time-consuming procurement tasks—from product research and supplier vetting to profit analysis—helping small businesses control costs and operate more efficiently.
Accio is Alibaba.com’s agentic AI workspace designed for SMEs and solo founders. Unlike standard chatbots that require constant prompting, Accio’s AI agents for e-commerce act as a digital operations team across the business lifecycle, handling market analysis, product design, sourcing, store optimisation and inventory monitoring.
European SMEs scale up on Alibaba.com
The rollout of free access to Accio Sourcing Expert, alongside a new, cost-effective “European SME Startup Pack” combining core sourcing and design tools, comes as European businesses increasingly turn to digital platforms to drive growth. New data shows European sellers on Alibaba.com now list 1.28 million products, up 78% compared to the same period last year.
The figures highlight how European SMEs are actively seizing new trade opportunities and using Alibaba.com and Accio’s infrastructure to scale their operations without increasing overheads.
50% lower xost, dfull AI power
For most small businesses, the primary hurdle to adopting advanced AI is cost. However, a recent 107-task benchmark evaluation released by Alibaba.com comparing Accio against general-purpose agents, including OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code, showed that Accio matches the task-completion quality of leading models at around 50%, making enterprise-grade automation realistic for SME budgets.
Turning AI curiosity into action at CoCreate Europe
Lowering the cost and complexity barrier is critical to closing the current SME adoption gap. Recent research conducted by Alibaba.com and Small Business Britain¹ shows that while only 5% of UK SMEs currently use agentic AI regularly, more than two-thirds (68%) want to learn how to apply it to their business.
To help bridge that gap between curiosity and execution, the two-day CoCreate Europe summit is dedicated to practical implementation. Alibaba.com will demonstrate on the ground how founders can use autonomous sourcing and e-commerce operations to “do more with less” in 2027, starting with an opening keynote from 16-year-old entrepreneur Harrison Nott, last year’s winner of the AI-driven CoCreate Pitch competition.
Patrick Sostmann, general manager Europe, Alibaba.com, said: “European SMEs are showing remarkable ambition, with products from European sellers on our platform surging 78% to 1.28 million. Yet while small businesses have an abundance of AI tools available to them, finding and integrating solutions that make a material difference to the bottom line remains a challenge. By opening up free access to Accio Sourcing Expert and launching our European SME Startup Pack, we are giving local businesses practical, agentic AI tools to lower their sourcing costs, do more with less, and compete on a global stage.”

items.title: JD Sports warns on profit again as France riots hit sales
items.summary: JD Sports has cut its profit target for the second time this year, this time blaming trading disruption caused by anti-government riots in France.  The FTSE 100 retailer, self-dubbed the ‘King of Trainers’, has slashed the top end of its profit expectations from £800m to £750m. The lower end, £700m, remains unchanged. An £800m pre-tax [...]
items.body:
JD Sports warns on profit again as France riots hit sales
JD Sports has cut its profit target for the second time this year, this time blaming trading disruption caused by anti-government riots in France.
The FTSE 100 retailer, self-dubbed the ‘King of Trainers’, has slashed the top end of its profit expectations from £800m to £750m. The lower end, £700m, remains unchanged. An £800m pre-tax profit would mark a 12 per cent drop from last year’s £852m.
Régis Schultz, who joined the group as chief executive in 2022, has been pushing to return the retailer to its Covid-era highs but has been beset by fragile consumer confidence and woes at Nike, a major supplier.
JD Sports posted a 2.7 per cent dip in like-for-like sales in Europe in the third quarter, a market which represents 34 per cent of its overall sales. Sales here in October were dragged down by “civil unrest, especially in France,” the firm said.
Major French cities, including Paris, have been beset by often-violent riots since 17 October, as students and activists protest a cost-of-living crisis and strained public services.
JD Sports said demand in Europe was also softened by this summer’s prolonged warm temperatures, as interest in winter and autumn clothing has only recently begun to pick up.
The trainer seller also saw sales slip in the UK, where demand has failed to keep pace with the levels seen during the FIFA World Cup this summer.
Like-for-like takings in this market, which accounts for 24 per cent of JD’s revenue, slipped by 2.6 per cent. Sales here also slowed due to low demand for winterwear and trainers, though the group’s outdoor business offset some of these declines.
‘No end in sight’ to declines
JD Sports has been struggling to boost demand in North America, its largest market. But the retailer’s declines have begun to slow, with negative sales growth easing slightly from -6.8 per cent in the second quarter to -2.2 per cent in the third.
This was helped by the retailer’s improved performance online, it said, “supported by better online ranges, focused marketing and controlled price investments”.
In September, JD announced plans to launch 140 stores in Mexico in a bid to boost its North American returns, eyeing the country’s large youth population.
The group saw its shares lose more than 10 per cent in one day in August after it cut its profit target from the initial £850m upper bound, blaming intense discounting among its rivals.
Analysts at Panmure Liberum said JD’s half-year update revealed “continued weak trading with no end in sight”. The stockbroker cut its profit targets for the company, questioning whether “cost savings alone will be sufficient to underpin consensus”.
Schultz told shareholders on Thursday: “In the UK and Europe, cooler weather in October began to bring through some of the autumn/winter demand delayed by unseasonably warm weather earlier in the quarter, although trading in Europe was affected by civil unrest.
“We are raising the bar on our product ranges, bringing new launches to market faster – particularly in apparel – and investing in a stronger, more seamless experience across stores and online,” he added.
Shares in JD Sports, which have gained eight per cent in the year to date, lost about one per cent to 93p in early trading.

items.body:
Lionsgate reports that a The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping hologram experience will debut in premium shopping destinations and movie theatres across the US today.
Partnering with Hologram Media Network (HMN) and Pretty Big Monster, an UNFOLD company (PBM), the campaign has officially rolled out at over 75 locations, and will be in market through to 30th November, leading into the film’s release in theatres on 20th November.
The interactive activation will bring holograms of two of The Hunger Games’ best known characters, Haymitch Abernathy and Effie Trinket, portrayed by Joseph Zada and Elle Fanning, to theatres, giving audiences a chance to come face-to-face with the film’s leading stars.
Filmed with the cast on set, the experience uses real-time AI transformation technology, shown on Proto Hologram displays via the Hologram Media Network. The campaign will roll-out across all of HMN’s current locations nationwide, with an additional 15 pop-up screens placed in theatres.
“We believe the most memorable experiences happen when people encounter something extraordinary in the places they already go to shop, see a movie or spend time together,” says Andrew Felts, CEO and Founder at Hologram Media Network. “With The Hunger Games, we’re bringing an experience typically reserved for a premiere into those everyday places nationwide, giving fans a chance to step into the story and leave with a memory worth sharing.”
“We’re always looking to bring audiences closer to the stories and characters they love, and this activation gives us the opportunity to do that in a completely new way,” says Jason Steinberg, Managing Director and Founder, Pretty Big Monster. “By combining our expertise with Lionsgate and HMN, we’re creating a moment that feels immersive, interactive and genuinely unexpected. Delivering it to audiences across the country makes the scale of the idea just as exciting as the technology behind it.”
From director Francis Lawrence, The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping follows 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) from District 12, beginning on the morning of the reaping for the 50th Annual Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell, the biggest Games yet with twice as many tributes.
Set in the world of Panem 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games, the story follows Haymitch into the arena, where he forms an unlikely alliance with fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace) and joins a coalition determined to challenge the Capitol’s control under President Snow (Ralph Fiennes). As the competition unfolds, Haymitch risks everything to take down the Games from within the arena, setting in motion the rebellion that will change Panem forever.
Based on Suzanne Collins’ best-selling novel, The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping also stars Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Maya Hawke, Whitney Peak, Kelvin Harrison Jr., and Ben Wang, produced by Nina Jacobson, Brad Simpson and Francis Lawrence with the screenplay by Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie.

items.title: Hotel Chocolat works with Astound Digital and Salesforce on launch of AI Gift Assistant
items.summary: Hotel Chocolat has launched an AI powered Gift Assistant on its website.This builds on the retailer's wider Christmas campaign, which starts with the person receiving the gift. A customer could ask, “find me a dark chocolate Christmas gift”. The assistant would then ask a follow up question and
items.body:
Hotel Chocolat has launched an AI powered Gift Assistant on its website.
This builds on the retailer's wider Christmas campaign, which starts with the person receiving the gift. A customer could ask, “find me a dark chocolate Christmas gift”. The assistant would then ask a follow up question and refine the shortlist as the customer shares more. From there, the customer can explore product details, choose from available pack sizes and gifting options, and add their selection to their basket.
Hotel Chocolat worked with Astound Digital and Salesforce on this. Salesforce Agentforce and Cimulate’s semantic search capability interpret a customer’s request and match it to product data in Salesforce Commerce Cloud. A customer can start with “a thank you for a host who loves dark chocolate”, refine the recommendations by adding a budget, then choose from available gifting options and add their selection to their basket within the same experience.
Martin Bell, Digital Director at Hotel Chocolat, says: “Search is becoming more conversational, and that’s changing what customers expect from a retailer’s website. We wanted to be on the front foot and make hotelchocolat.com a place people come for expert advice, inspiration and the confidence to choose a gift that feels right."
"In 11 weeks, together with Astound and Salesforce, we transformed the website experience with our new Gift Assistant, in time for our busiest gifting period. That means we can learn from real Christmas shopping decisions by seeing what people ask for, which recommendations they act on and where they still need help. What we learn will shape how we use conversational AI across Hotel Chocolat, including how we help customers discover our products when their search starts beyond our website.”
Emma Sahota, Managing Director UKI at Astound Digital, says: “The future of commerce isn't just about helping customers find products faster; it's about helping them make better decisions. By harnessing AI, Hotel Chocolat is bringing the expertise of its in-store teams into the online shopping journey, making gifting more intuitive, personal and effortless."
"It's a great example of what's possible when retailers combine a clear customer vision with the right technology and delivery expertise, creating a strong foundation for continued innovation.”
Hotel Chocolat will use the Christmas trading period to assess how the assistant shapes product discovery. Those findings will inform further functionality planned for early 2027 and the retailer's wider strategy for large language models (LLMs).

items.title: dm-drogerie markt ramps up Vusion partnership as it looks to digitalise stores across Germany
items.summary: Vusion has announced an expansion of its partnership with dm-drogerie markt, a European drugstore retailer. The agreement covers the deployment of the newest EdgeSense platform in about 2,000 stores in Germany over the next three years.dm has more than 4,200 stores across Europe and was na
items.body:
Vusion has announced an expansion of its partnership with dm-drogerie markt, a European drugstore retailer. The agreement covers the deployment of the newest EdgeSense platform in about 2,000 stores in Germany over the next three years.
dm has more than 4,200 stores across Europe and was named Germany’s favourite retailer in EY-Parthenon’s 2026 Retail Performance Ranking. The Vusion platform will help it optimise the productivity and quality of in-store processes such as pricing, picking of online orders, replenishment, etc. The objective is to achieve perfect price integrity, accelerate e-commerce and improve on-shelf availability.
Beyond these initial use cases, dm and Vusion aim to deepen their R&D collaboration to develop new shopping experiences. The product and location signals generated by EdgeSense will provide a data foundation for context aware AI agents that can understand shoppers’ requests and help them find relevant products within the store.
“We want every visit to dm to be easy, enjoyable and relevant to our customers’ needs. Technology should give our colleagues more freedom to focus on customers and make their daily work easier," comments Christoph Werner, Chairman of the Management Board at dm-drogerie markt.
"With Vusion, we are creating the digital foundation to do this at scale, connecting our shelves with the information and services our teams need. Our customers will also find their way around our stores, discover the right products and access useful information. Our shared ambition is to develop technology around the way people want to shop."
“dm’s decision demonstrates how central connected stores have become to retail’s future. Working with a retailer recognised for its customer focus shows how digitalisation can strengthen the qualities that make physical retail successful. By connecting products, locations and store teams, we can improve execution today and build the real-world data foundation for AI agents to deliver new value tomorrow and enable connected shopping experiences,” says Thierry Gadou, Chairman and CEO at Vusion.
EdgeSense will create a digital map of products across dm’s stores, with a view to enabling new services that make shopping easier and more intuitive. Precise product location will provide the foundation for indoor navigation, helping shoppers find the items they need more quickly. For store colleagues, the same capabilities will simplify product searches and online order preparation, giving them more time for advice and personal service.
At the same time, EdgeSense will also interact with robots deployed in stores by Ubica to enhance store operations and customer service.

items.title: THG Fulfil doubles AutoStore capacity at its Omega warehouse in Warrington, UK
items.summary: THG Fulfil, an AutoStore distributor and provider of SaaS technology, robotics, and operations platforms built for global e-commerce, has announced a capacity expansion at its Omega warehouse in Warrington. Just over a year after the original 120,000-bin installation, it has doubled the warehou
items.body:
THG Fulfil, an AutoStore distributor and provider of SaaS technology, robotics, and operations platforms built for global e-commerce, has announced a capacity expansion at its Omega warehouse in Warrington.
Just over a year after the original 120,000-bin installation, it has doubled the warehouse’s storage capacity to 240,000 bins. The move elevates the Omega’s AutoStore storage capacity from 4.2 million units to 8.4 million units, supported by 64 high-speed carousel ports and a total of 184 energy efficient R5 robots, representing an increase of 84 robots from the initial launch.
This physical infrastructure integrates with THG Fulfil’s proprietary technology suite, which includes a warehouse management system (WMS), warehouse control system (WCS), and courier management platform (CMP).
THG Fulfil says that it stands as the only AutoStore distributor globally that is also an active end user of the technology, operating one of the highest output D2C (direct-to-consumer) fulfilment facilities among AutoStore deployments worldwide. This experience spans a connected global network of automated facilities, including within THG Fulfil’s US facility in New Jersey, enabling retailers to scale their physical and digital commerce operations across multiple continents.
