items.title: Bloom & Wild veteran Stephen Janaway seeks next senior retail technology leadership role
items.summary: After nine years, Stephen Janaway is moving on from Bloom & Wild where he has served as VP Engineering.In a LinkedIn post, Janaway, whose CV also includes stints at Net-a-Porter and Nokia, said: "I joined back in 2017 when the Technology team was a single squad and Bloom & Wild was one brand
items.body:
After nine years, Stephen Janaway is moving on from Bloom & Wild where he has served as VP Engineering.
In a LinkedIn post, Janaway, whose CV also includes stints at Net-a-Porter and Nokia, said: "I joined back in 2017 when the Technology team was a single squad and Bloom & Wild was one brand with ambitions well beyond its size. To have been part of taking the company from that point to acquiring and integrating new brands, expanding internationally, and building genuine scale has been one of the most rewarding experiences of my career. The journey wasn't always straightforward, but that's what made it interesting."
He added: "I want to say a particular thank you to Aron Gelbard (Co-founder and CEO) for giving me the opportunity and for the trust he has placed in me over the years. And to everyone I've worked with across the business - thank you! The team at Bloom & Wild is genuinely one of the best I've encountered, and it's been a privilege to be part of it."
"A special mention to the Technology team. It has been an honour to lead such a talented, committed and genuinely lovely group of people. Everything the company has achieved technically has been down to you."
Janaway is now looking for his next senior technology leadership role, and says that he would like to work with a team that wants to use AI well. He concluded: "At Bloom & Wild I defined and led our AI transformation across Product Engineering, and I’d love to take what I’ve learnt into my next role. If you’re hiring, or think we should talk, please get in touch."

items.title: The DIY and hardware retail market hits $3.09 trillion in 2026
items.summary: The global DIY market reached US$3.09 trillion in 2026 at a CAGR of 2.40%. Traditional DIY home improvement trends are stabilising, and smart home improvements are the fastest-growing niche at a 10.03% CAGR.What’s Driving Recent Growth?42% of people now classify themselves as pur
items.body:
The global DIY market reached US$3.09 trillion in 2026 at a CAGR of 2.40%. Traditional DIY home improvement trends are stabilising, and smart home improvements are the fastest-growing niche at a 10.03% CAGR.
What’s Driving Recent Growth?
42% of people now classify themselves as pure DIYers, keeping hardware stores packed, even during housing slowdowns. Influencers have a big part to play here. Accounts like Charlie DIY offer step-by-step guidance on how to complete household repairs, and Gosforth Handyman gives practical advice on how to tackle complex improvements.
Around the House with Eric G and The DIY Guys Podcast are other examples of how DIY content is finding new audiences. Classic stories, like The Three Little Pigs, are also still prominent. Those who have an understanding of Huff and Puff slot games will know that the theme is based around the fairy tale and features the pigs, wolf, and construction materials.
In the modern age, the story is more relevant than ever. The pigs invest time, effort, and equity into building a more durable house, which in this case is made out of stone, an upgrade from brick in the classic tale.
This reflects the current trend of people reinvesting their capital into their property. The housing market slowing down has led to people fortifying what they have to build equity, rather than simply relying on moving up the housing ladder.
High mortgage rates have also led to people improving the house they have. Trends like this have had a knock-on effect across DIY stores. Home Depot, for example, grew its sales from 2.5% to 4.5% in 2026.
Lowe's is experiencing an annual growth rate of 6%, and Wickes also reported a group revenue increase of 4.5%. Wickes has plans to expand their network, growing to 300 stores and adding 5fivenew outlets this year. The company has plans to open 10 stores per year from 2028. TradePro, which operates under Wickes, saw an 8% rise in sales too, showing how much growth there is within the sector.
Remote and Hybrid Work is Helping the Retail Sector
High housing costs and a scarcity of new inventory have helped to drive property prices, and for a lot of people, building an extension or converting a loft is now more affordable than paying the high fees associated with buying real estate.
Working from home is now a permanent fixture for millions of people across the world. Homeowners are now renovating so they can create dedicated home offices and privacy screens.
It’s not just the DIY retail market that's growing either. The global office furniture market is also growing, and reached $984.36 billion in 2026. As more people work from home, shopper appetite has surged. Instead of relying on weekly shops, many people make shorter, more frequent trips to the supermarket, which is helping local independent stores and neighbourhood branches.
Ripple effects also include retail stores that sell comfortable lounge clothing, with many experiencing record breaking profits due to changing consumer habits. Trends like this are supporting the retail sector and having a monumental influence on expansion and growth.

items.title: General Pants Co enters voluntary administration, putting hundreds of jobs at risk
items.summary: Australian fashion chain becomes latest retailer in trouble after David Jones, Cue and Veronika Maine Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The youth fashion chain General Pants Co has become the latest major retailer to slide into voluntary administration, putting nearly 500 jobs at risk as Australia’s retail sector continues to struggle with cash-strapped shoppers and online-only competitors. The collapse comes not long after that of the upmarket department store David Jones and premium womenswear brands Cue and Veronika Maine, underscoring the mounting toll of tough economic conditions on established retailers. Continue reading...
items.body:
The youth fashion chain General Pants Co has become the latest major retailer to slide into voluntary administration, putting nearly 500 jobs at risk as Australia’s retail sector continues to struggle with cash-strapped shoppers and online-only competitors.
The collapse comes not long after that of the upmarket department store David Jones and premium womenswear brands Cue and Veronika Maine, underscoring the mounting toll of tough economic conditions on established retailers.
The consultancy Alvarez & Marsal confirmed it had taken control of General Pants Co and nine related businesses after being appointed their voluntary administrator late on Wednesday evening.
In a statement, the administrators said they were working closely with the existing management team to undertake an urgent assessment of the business, including its trading performance, stores, stock and costs.
All 35 General Pants Co stores and its online store would remain open and trading as usual while the administrators worked out whether they could sell or restructure the business to keep it afloat, the firm said.
A spokesperson for General Pants Co’s parent company, Alquemie Group, said it had progressively cut the number of physical stores due to the “recent Australian retail trading environment, and rapid structural changes in the sector, including the growing dominance of offshore online-only retailers”.
They said they had tried a “range of options” to save General Pants Co from administration, including attempting to sell the business or securing a “significant capital injection” to help it better compete against large scale competitors.
“None were ultimately viable,” they said.
They said the voluntary administration process will examine whether General Pants Co could be restructured into a smaller scale, “more focussed” and, ultimately, viable business.
Alvarez & Marsal said the 500 people employed by General Pants Co across Australia and New Zealand would continue to be paid for the work they did during the administration period.
Additionally, the consultancy said staff entitlements accrued prior to the appointment remained legally protected under the Corporations Act and of a higher priority to administrators than “most” other unsecured creditor claims.
Two of the Alvarez & Marsal managing directors, Jason Tracy and Glen Kanevsky, were appointed to oversee the administration, with a first meeting with creditors due to be held on 30 November.
Tracy described General Pants Co as “one of Australia’s best-known youth fashion brands, with a loyal customer base and a dedicated team”.
He said the administrators’ immediate priorities were to keep the stores trading, support employees and customers, and pursue “a sale and/or recapitalisation” of the business.
“With Black Friday next week, we are focused on maximising trading performance and expect strong demand over the period,” Tracy said.
“We thank the team members, landlords and suppliers of General Pants Co for their support as we work through the administration.”
Retailers under pressure
General Pants Co, which began in 1972 as a specialty denim store on Sydney’s George Street and has traded across Australia and New Zealand since, is not the only Australian retailer under significant pressure.
Last week, the embattled upmarket retailer David Jones entered administration with more than $400m owed to creditors. Less than two months earlier Cue Clothing Co, the owner of mainstay Australian labels Cue and Veronika Maine, entered administration and receivership in September.
Last year Mosaic Group, the owner of brands including Noni B, Rivers, and Katies, was liquidated.
While Australian retailers deal with their own increased operating costs, indebted households are tightened their budgets during a new bout of inflationary pressures.
This strain is driving a sharp contraction across the sector, according to the credit reporting agency Equifax, marked by surging business closures and a slowdown in new brands.
Equifax’s Brad Walters said that the strain was not limited to large retailers such as David Jones.
“Smaller retailers are also dealing with a difficult combination of softer discretionary spending, rising operating costs and increasingly narrow financial buffers,” Walters said.
“Instead of funding long-term expansion, smaller operators are taking on credit simply to manage immediate overheads.”
While David Jones is closing half of its 38 stores, rival Myer is facing its own financial stress, with the chain forced to offer “higher than planned promotional activity to stimulate demand”.
Four out of Myer’s five newly acquired apparel chains – Jay Jays, Portmans, Dotti, and Jacqui E – recorded falling sales last financial year, leaving Just Jeans as the sole brand to post growth.

items.title: Dorset police in illegal tobacco crackdown
items.summary: Dorset police have this month raided more than 42 premises, including convenience stores, in Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole, Dorset, seizing nearly 140,000 illicit cigarettes. The force reported this week that it had made five arrests and taken £7,869 in cash as well as the 138,640… This story continues at Dorset police in illegal tobacco crackdown Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The force reported this week that it had made five arrests and taken £7,869 in cash as well as the 138,640 cigarettes, worth an estimated £140,000.
Dorset Police worked alongside local authorities trading standards teams, as well as the South West regional organised crime unit and tax authorities to disrupt suspected crime networks exploiting high street businesses.
Kieron Wilson, Bournemouth council cabinet member with responsibility for trading standards, said: “This work shows we won’t tolerate shops that undercut the many local traders in our towns that do play by the rules
“These operations – in partnership with the National Crime Agency and Dorset Police – have directly targeted organised criminal activity that affects our communities and undermines confidence in our town and district centres.
“Our trading standards team will continue to take similar action and our message to those operating illegally is simple; you are not welcome on our high street.”
Dorset police and crime commissioner David Sidwick said: “High-street crime can have a significant impact on our communities, undermining legitimate businesses, affecting people’s confidence and damaging the places we live and work.
“This operation demonstrates Dorset Police’s commitment to tackling criminality that can hide behind seemingly legitimate businesses.”

The last Sainsbury’s to open was in Carrickfergus, County Antrim, in… This story continues at First Northern Ireland opening since 2009 for Sainsbury’s Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The 32,208sq ft site is the group’s first-ever store in Omagh, County Tyrone, and its 13th in the region.
The last Sainsbury’s to open was in Carrickfergus, County Antrim, in 2009.
The store is in Omagh’s Great Northern Retail Park, and open from 8am to 10pm Monday to Saturday and 1pm to 6pm on Sundays.
It represents a multi-million-pound investment in the local economy and has created 130 jobs for people in and around Omagh.
The new store will also be a base for Sainsbury’s groceries online, which launches in a few weeks.
The added geographical coverage means all customers in Northern Ireland will have access to the retailer’s home delivery service for the first time.
The store’s opening is part of Sainsbury’s broader expansion plans across the UK.
David Pilbeam, Sainsbury’s director of acquisitions, capital projects and engineering, said: “We’re really excited to have opened our 13th store in Northern Ireland, demonstrating our commitment to growing our presence here and allowing us to bring Sainsbury’s to Omagh for the very first time.
“We’ve completely revitalised two units in Great Northern Retail Park in the process and we hope everyone in the community is as pleased with the result as we are.”
As part of its opening, Sainsbury’s gave £5,000 to sponsor breakfast clubs at five local primary schools.

items.title: David Beckham's perfume, Poundland – and a mighty, mighty stink | Arwa Mahdawi
items.summary: The Beckhams have made an art of monetising their every move. But apparently there are limits to where they’re prepared to sell their wares Thoughts and half-price prayers with Poundland, please. The discount chain has been on the verge of collapse for a while , and its future looks bleak. Now, to add to the ignominy, David Beckham is kicking it while it’s down. Not literally, by the way: I suppose I should spell that out since we’re dealing with a litigious billionaire . I did not mean to imply or cause a reasonable person to infer that Sir David is standing on Brixton high street kicking a Poundland. Rather, DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, is causing a bit of a stink about the fact that the football legend’s fragrance range was found on sale in the discount store as well as at other purveyors of budget goods. It is now suing the perfume company , Coty, which it further accuses of under reporting sales, for $41m (£31m). Do you have an opinion on the issues raised
items.body:
Thoughts and half-price prayers with Poundland, please. The discount chain has been on the verge of collapse for a while, and its future looks bleak. Now, to add to the ignominy, David Beckham is kicking it while it’s down.
Not literally, by the way: I suppose I should spell that out since we’re dealing with a litigious billionaire. I did not mean to imply or cause a reasonable person to infer that Sir David is standing on Brixton high street kicking a Poundland. Rather, DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, is causing a bit of a stink about the fact that the football legend’s fragrance range was found on sale in the discount store as well as at other purveyors of budget goods. It is now suing the perfume company, Coty, which it further accuses of under reporting sales, for $41m (£31m).
“DB Ventures … ensures that all of its brand licensing partnerships maintain the lifestyle and luxury image of the brand that Sir David has carefully cultivated for decades,” court filings stated. “Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station. How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.” Coty has denied that it had ever sold the fragrances in Poundland.
Either way, the lawyer who wrote this exquisite paragraph is wasted in the legal profession and should really think about a marketing career. They’ve managed to distill the essence of the Beckham brand in just a few words: desperation and greed.
I’m not saying that Victoria and David Beckham, who are now worth an estimated £1.2bn, aren’t talented and hardworking, etc. But at a certain point monetising every second of your life, and wringing every possible penny out of your famous name, gets a bit naff, doesn’t it? While celebrity-backed businesses and endorsements are obviously commonplace, the Beckhams have taken things to an extreme, slapping their name or image on everything from whisky to Walkers crisps to AliExpress. Even 15-year-old Harper Beckham is launching a skincare brand. They’ve become the British Kardashian-Jenners.
Not everyone in the Beckham family seems quite so keen on the family business, however. “My family values public promotion and endorsements above all else,” Brooklyn Peltz Beckham, who has been in a bitter feud with his parents, lamented in a statement published in January. “Brand Beckham comes first.” You’d think that a public feud with their son would have taught Posh ‘n’ Becks that there are certain things money can’t buy. For everything else, there’s Poundland.
Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January
items.summary: Government under pressure to help households as increase would add £443 to average annual dual-fuel bill Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers Tell us: are you shopping around for a better deal? UK inflation rises to 3.6% Energy bills across Great Britain are predicted to reach £2,166 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East conflict piles pressure on the government to offer more support to hard-hit households. The government’s cap on gas and electricity prices is likely to rise by 26% early next year, equivalent to adding £443 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, in one of the biggest quarterly price rises on record, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight. Continue reading...
items.body:
Energy bills across Great Britain are predicted to reach £2,166 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East conflict piles pressure on the government to offer more support to hard-hit households.
The government’s cap on gas and electricity prices is likely to rise by 26% early next year, equivalent to adding £443 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, in one of the biggest quarterly price rises on record, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight.
The dire prediction for millions of hard-pressed households marks the final forecast before the industry regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, sets electricity and gas rates for the coldest months of the year from January through to March via a new energy price cap next Wednesday.
The forecast was well above Cornwall’s prediction in late September that the cap would rise by 16% to £1,999 a year from January. Bills are expected to be even higher after an increase in gas market prices through October because of escalating violence in the Middle East and deepening fears over Europe’s gas storage levels.
Figures released by the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday showed the headline rate of inflation rose to 3.6% in October, up from 3.5% in September, after petrol prices rose and diesel hit a record high.
Craig Lowrey, the retail markets principal at Cornwall Insight, said: “After already climbing in October, energy bills look set to rise again in the new year, and the timing could hardly be worse, with colder weather in January pushing up energy use and households already dealing with the cost of living crisis.
“Once again, the cause lies thousands of miles away, yet another reminder of how events beyond our control have a very real impact on our energy bills.”
The energy price rise will come as a blow to the government after the chancellor, John Healey, promised to set “a new course to get energy costs down in line with Europe” in his maiden budget last month.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said: “I know that the price of energy bills this winter weighs heavily on struggling families up and down the country. Access to energy is an everyday essential and not a luxury, which is why we have taken immediate action to give people breathing space.”
The assurance echoes Healey’s budget which promised “breathing space” to struggling households this winter through a one-off payment of £100 in January for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D.
The £2.6bn “household energy payment” will go directly into bank accounts to “take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people through to the spring”, according to Healey.
The payment will be in addition to the warm home discount, which offers about six million means-tested households in England, Wales and Scotland £150 off winter fuel bills.
The move follows a string of cuts to electricity levies over the past year, which have shaved about £150 a year off costs. The Treasury also promised to keep the 5% VAT levy off electricity bills for 29 million households until July, extending the annual savings to £50 a year.
Fahnbulleh said: “Affordability is my number one priority, and I will continue driving towards cheap, clean power.”

items.title: Locker milestone makes Tesco InPost’s largest retail partner network in the UK
items.summary: InPost reports a milestone with Tesco, installing its 1,650th locker across the grocery giant's UK estate to become its largest network with any single retail partner in the UK.According to InPost's customer research, 66% of its locker users combine their visit with a Tesco shop and 53% now visit th
items.body:
InPost reports a milestone with Tesco, installing its 1,650th locker across the grocery giant's UK estate to become its largest network with any single retail partner in the UK.
According to InPost's customer research, 66% of its locker users combine their visit with a Tesco shop and 53% now visit the retailer more often because of the locker. Satisfaction is high too, with 75% of users saying their visit was more convenient because of the locker, with the majority rating the service ten out of ten and stating they would recommend it to a friend or colleague.
The milestone builds on a partnership with Tesco that began in 2021, with InPost lockers now installed across the retailer's different store formats, from Express to Extra and Superstores.
Paul Selvey, Network Director at InPost UK, says: “Reaching this locker milestone with Tesco shows just how much shoppers value having real choice over how they collect, send and return parcels. For years, delivery has been designed around cost and convenience at checkout, not around what actually works for the consumer receiving the parcel. Putting lockers across Tesco Express locations to its Extra stores, means that choice is built into the consumer’s shopping journey itself, rather than bolted on as an afterthought."
Nick Burrows, Head of Property Income at Tesco, says: “We’re always looking for ways to make the shopping trip more convenient for customers. With 1,650 InPost lockers now available across Tesco stores, more customers than ever can collect, return or send parcels at a time that suits them, all from their local store. It’s another way we’re helping customers save time and fit everyday tasks around their busy lives."
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
OOH delivery was a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world. Our winners were revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
The event consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.

items.title: A potato war has been simmering for decades between the US and Japan. It’s about to reach boiling point
items.summary: Under pressure from Donald Trump, Japan’s government could be about to lift a ban on imported American potatoes, which farmers say would threaten their livelihoods It could be a piping hot croquette eaten on the go, a bowl of nikujaga stew or a plate of home-cooked chips. One culinary thread runs through them all – the Japanese potato. Along with rice , the crop is fiercely protected as one of only a few homegrown staples in a country that imports more than 60% of its food. Continue reading...
items.body:
It could be a piping hot croquette eaten on the go, a bowl of nikujaga stew or a plate of home-cooked chips. One culinary thread runs through them all – the Japanese potato.
Along with rice, the crop is fiercely protected as one of only a few homegrown staples in a country that imports more than 60% of its food.
But that could be about to change. Under pressure from Donald Trump, Japan is moving towards lifting a 76-year-old ban on imported American potatoes.
Japan’s potato farmers say lifting the ban would threaten their livelihoods, and expose consumers to an inferior product. They worry batches of American potatoes could bring harmful insects and pests into Japanese fields.
Tokyo partially lifted the ban in 2006 to permit imports of US potatoes exclusively to make crisps. The vegetables must be transported in sealed containers and then cooked at a high temperature to prevent the spread of pests and diseases.
But a complete lifting of the ban would put fresh American potatoes on restaurant menus and supermarket shelves for the first time since 1950.
“We have repeatedly and unequivocally stated our opposition to imports,” said Toshihide Numasawa, an employee of the Japan Agriculture group in Hokkaido, where about 80% of the country’s potatoes are grown. He said there were various reasons for the objection, including the “risk of pests and diseases entering the country and damage to Hokkaido’s production areas.”
Crunch time
Potatoes were initially collector’s items for intrigued plant enthusiasts when Dutch traders introduced them to Japan in 1598. By the mid-1800s, potatoes were a nutritious alternative to rice – a crop unsuited to Hokkaido’s cooler climate. Now they are the basis for the perennial favourite jaga bata, a baked version slathered in butter, while poteto sarada has practically achieved national-dish status.
Hokkaido’s best-known variety is the Danshaku (Irish Cobbler), a potato high in starch whose fluffy, absorbent flesh makes them perfect for butter and other toppings or to soak up meat juices in a stew.
“We believe consumers have come to recognise which are best suited to particular dishes,” said Numasawa, adding that Hokkaido potato farmers were also being buffeted by homegrown pest outbreaks, global heating and rural depopulation.
The country now grows more than 90 varieties of potato and Japanese consumers ate 3.5m tons of potatoes in 2024, according to the agriculture ministry, among them 1.2m tons of fresh imports used to make crisps.
The tuber’s place at the centre of Japan-US trade negotiations has created an early headache for Japan’s new agriculture minister, Arata Takebe, whose constituency is located in prime potato-growing country in Hokkaido.
The plan to lift the ban “should progress after thorough scientific and technical discussion” Takebe recently told Jiji Press, adding that a decision could take “considerable time”.
“I know the [US] side has strong expectations, but the ban on imports will not be lifted without sufficient discussions or an agreement acceptable to both sides,” he said.
While potatoes imported for crisps are subject to strict quarantine measures, farmers fear batches of imported fresh potatoes could bring in harmful insects and microbes. Japan’s government has identified 21 pests and diseases that could pose a risk of invasion.
The potato cyst nematode and pale potato cyst nematode are causing most concern. Although they are not a threat to human health, they can damage the vegetable’s roots, which stunts their growth, and remain present in soil for more than 15 years.
Earlier this year, congressional lawmakers urged Trump to continue raising the ban with the Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.
“US potato growers produce the best potatoes in the world,” they wrote in a letter. “Japan represents a massive market with significant export opportunities for American potato growers.”
After raising the issue during his first term in office, Trump has persuaded Japan’s government to begin talks as he faces accusations that his policies have been “disastrous” for rural America.
Supporters of lifting the ban say it would lower prices for Japanese consumers and bring American farmers an additional $150m a year in export earnings.
But farmers in Hokkaido claim that not enough has been done to eliminate the threat from pests and disease.
“Protecting Hokkaido’s agriculture is not just about protecting Hokkaido,” the Hokkaido Agricultural Corporations Association said in a statement. “It also means protecting the production base that will support Japan’s food supply for the future.”
Naohiro Makino, a potato farmer in Hokkaido, said the ban on fresh potatoes should stay. “Once pests get in, you can’t grow potatoes for more than a decade,” he told the Asahi Shimbun newspaper. “For the sake of the farmland our ancestors protected, I am firmly opposed [to lifting the ban].”

items.title: Scottish convenience sector ‘squeezed to breaking point’
items.summary: The amount that Scottish convenience stores invest in their businesses has fallen for the second year in a row, according the to the Scottish Grocers’ Federation (SGF). The decline in investment from £94m in 2024 to £70m in 2026 was revealed as the SGF prepared… This story continues at Scottish convenience sector ‘squeezed to breaking point’ Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The decline in investment from £94m in 2024 to £70m in 2026 was revealed as the SGF prepared to kick off its conference in Glasgow this morning with the federation’s annual report on the sector.
The fall in investment was attributed to the financial pressure under which convenience stores are operating.
Despite the decline, there was an increase in the number of convenience stores in Scotland over the past year, up by 39 stores to 5,267, with the number of employees in the sector remaining static at 49,000.
The SGF says cost pressures such as above-inflation hikes in employment costs, retail crime, tighter regulations across a range of product areas and a real-terms decline in business rates relief have resulted in retailers being forced to cut services and increase prices for customers.
SGF chief executive Pete Cheema said: “Our local shops are fighting for survival. Every increase in costs, every new regulatory burden and every incident of retail crime strips more money away from investment in businesses that communities depend upon.
“The sharp decline in store investment is not just a statistic, it is evidence of a sector being squeezed to breaking point.
“When community retailers stop investing in their future, it is a sign they are struggling to survive in the present.”
Despite this, Cheema added that convenience stores continued to play a vital role in community life.
He said: “SGF’s Local Shop Report highlights the sector’s contribution and the pressures threatening its future, underlining the need for targeted government support and a more joined-up approach to policy and regulation.
“Retailers need the confidence and financial headroom to invest in their businesses, support staff and continue delivering for the communities they serve.”

items.title: As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
items.summary: China worries the scandal could ramp up pressure on the US to further restrict the sale of advanced chips.
items.body:
As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
- Published
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.
For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.
Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.
Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.
The BBC has approached the White House for comment.
Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".
"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.
The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".
Another 'spy balloon' incident?
For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.
The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.
It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.
Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim, advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.
Now that opening may be under threat.
History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.
Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.
But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.
The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.
"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.
"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.
The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.
"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.
Trump-Xi summit unlikely to collapse
Both Trump and Xi have significant incentives to keep talking.
China's economy remains under pressure and is increasingly reliant on exports. Xi needs trade to keep flowing and this meeting is a key stepping stone to replacing the current trade truce that is due to expire in January.
Meanwhile Trump has repeatedly touted his close relationship with Xi and argued that maintaining dialogue is essential to managing competition between the two powers.
The US president is in his last two years and faces an uphill struggle to pass domestic legislation after the midterms. To counter this, he could be looking for some foreign policy wins.
He may also hope for Xi's help to end the war in the Middle East.
Neither side will want to be discussing intelligence concerns and technology controls instead of trade, investment and economic co-operation.
The summit is also being carefully choreographed by Beijing to show off its technological prowess in Shenzhen - a deeply symbolic choice of city.
It's home to some of the country's biggest tech companies and has become a showcase for Beijing's ambitions in AI and advanced manufacturing.
Also, given Washington's tighter restrictions on advanced chips, Beijing has options for retaliation.
One of its most powerful tools is its dominance of key rare earth minerals. China processes much of the world's supply for materials that are used in everything from electric vehicles and smartphones to military equipment.
Analysts have long warned that technological restrictions can trigger a cycle of retaliation in which each side reaches for its strongest economic leverage.
That would shift the current trend of US-China relations from engagement back towards mutual suspicion.
